In Psalms, it qualifies believers who are faithful to the Lord, those who persevere in piety. In the Pentateuch (Deuteronomy), it marks the contrast with Israel's unfaithfulness. In 2 Samuel 20:19, the city calls for trust by describing itself as "faithful in Israel." The word thus shifts from the concrete (a reliable messenger) to the ethical and religious (loyalty to God).
H0529.portee: This word reminds us that faithfulness is not a rare or mysterious quality: it is constant loyalty, both small and great, in what is entrusted to us. For a believer, it means remaining attached to God and His promises even when it is difficult. It also touches our daily lives: in our words (like a witness), our missions (like a messenger), our commitments. God shows Himself faithful to us; He asks us to respond with the same integrity.

sens: Quality of one who keeps their promises and remains constant in their commitments
Stability, firmness, absence of wavering
Truth, accuracy, conformity to reality
Reliability in the execution of a charge or function
H0530.detail:
1. Faithfulness is the quality of one who firmly keeps their promises and commitments to someone. It is remaining loyal and enduring in a relationship or commitment. For example, Moses' hands "remained steady" thanks to the constant support of Aaron and Hur (Exodus 17:12), or God swears to David that He will keep His faithfulness toward him (Psalms 89:50).
2. It is also stability and firmness — the absence of wavering or change. The earth "remains firm" because God founded it in His faithfulness which "endures from generation to generation" (Psalms 119:90). This is what makes something solid and lasting.
3. The word also means truth: the word that conforms to reality, without lies or deception. The righteous "speaks the truth" (Proverbs 12:17), and God "declares His truth" (Psalms 40:11) — He proclaims what is real and reliable.
4. Finally, it is reliability in the exercise of a charge: one who fulfills their function seriously, without diversion or negligence. The priests in charge of the treasury of the house of the Lord acted "with faithfulness and with integrity of heart" (2 Chronicles 19:9).
H0530.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be firm, solid, durable." This same root gives the verb "to believe" or "to trust" — for to believe someone, one must judge them firm, stable, worthy of trust. It is also the origin of "Amen," which means "so be it": one affirms that something is true and lasting. Faithfulness is thus, at its core, the solidity and permanence of one who keeps their word.
H0530.emploi: The word appears 49 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms (30 occurrences), which celebrate God's faithfulness to His people and His promises. It also appears in historical accounts (1 and 2 Chronicles, 2 Kings), where it qualifies the scrupulous management of sacred charges and treasures. Proverbs uses it to speak of the righteous who tell the truth. Isaiah and Jeremiah use it to denounce the absence of faithfulness and truth among the unfaithful. Its meaning revolves around four axes: God's faithfulness to His promises (Psalms 89:2-3), the unshakeable stability of His character (Psalms 119:90), the truth of His word (Psalms 40:11), and the diligence of servants in their functions (2 Chronicles 19:9, 31:12).
H0530.portee: This word reminds Christians that God is completely reliable. He always keeps His promises, never changes, and His word is absolutely true — one can rest entirely on it. It is a foundation of trust and peace for the believer. It also invites every disciple to imitate this faithfulness: by honoring their commitments, speaking the truth, and serving diligently in their responsibilities.

sens: Father of the prophet Isaiah
H0531.detail: 1. Amoz is the father of the great prophet Isaiah, whose name means "strong" or "mighty." He is mentioned several times in the Bible, always as "Isaiah, son of Amoz," which shows the importance of his lineage. He is first encountered in 2 Kings 19:2, when the messengers of King Hezekiah go to consult the prophet Isaiah.
H0531.origine: The name Amoz comes from Hebrew and literally means "strong" or "mighty." This name belongs to the same family as the verb "to be strong." Although few details are given about Amoz himself, he is primarily defined by his fatherhood of the prophet Isaiah, one of the greatest prophets of the Old Testament.
H0531.emploi: Amoz appears 13 times in the Hebrew Bible, always for the purpose of identifying the prophet Isaiah as his son. He is found in the books of Kings (2 Kings 19:2, 2 Kings 20:1), in Chronicles (2 Chronicles 32:20), and especially in the book of the prophet Isaiah himself (Isaiah 1:1, 13:1, 37:2, 38:1), where the formula "Isaiah, son of Amoz" introduces the various prophecies. No other actions of Amoz are reported; he lives only through his son.

sens: Descendant of Amon, servant of Solomon
H0532.detail: Ami is a man who lived during the time of the Exile and the Return, mentioned only once in the Bible. He appears in the list of descendants of the servants of Solomon who returned from captivity in Babylon with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:57). His name is also referred to as Amon in another parallel text (Nehemiah 7:59), suggesting that these two forms refer to the same person or family.
H0532.origine: The name Ami means "servant" or "slave" in Hebrew. It comes from a root that expresses the idea of being bound or subjected. It is a theophoric or descriptive name, typical of Hebrew names that indicate a person's condition or social status. The variant Amon (אָמוֹן) is an alternative form of the same name.
H0532.emploi: Ami is a minor character in the Return from Exile. He is cited in the context of the families who left Babylon to return to Jerusalem after the destruction of the Temple in 586 B.C. He is specifically named as the son of a family of temple servants, indicating that he came from a class of workers serving in worship. His appearance in this genealogical list shows that even humble servants of Solomon have been recorded in sacred history.

sens: One who possesses great physical or moral strength
One who has considerable means to act
One who demonstrates vigor, resilience
One who has courage, boldness
H0533.detail:
1. The word describes someone or something that has real strength, capable of accomplishing great things: God is mighty in His creation (Isaiah 40:26, where His "mighty power" keeps the stars in order), and a mighty warrior can terrify his enemies (Isaiah 28:2 depicts a "strong and mighty" scourge like a devastating hurricane).
2. It also refers to what has weight, influence, and the ability to grow or impose itself: a conspiracy becomes "mighty" when it grows and gains support (2 Samuel 15:12), just like a movement that acquires political or military power.
3. The word can evoke the absence of weakness, the ability to stand firm in the face of adversity: Job acknowledges that God is "almighty" in the face of strength, meaning invincible and unparalleled (Job 9:4 and 9:19).
4. In a military context, it characterizes the brave warrior who does not flee, even in the heart of danger: only "the most courageous" dares to face battle, while others flee (Amos 2:16).
H0533.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of muscular strength or driving power. It is related to other terms that denote vigor, courage, and firmness. In biblical Hebrew, words from this family are used to speak of a person's physical strength, the power of an army, or the divine ability to act. The underlying image is that of concentrated strength, capable of production or destruction.
H0533.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the books of poetry and prophecy. It is first used for God: His power is limitless and guarantees the order of the cosmos (Isaiah 40:26). It also describes devastating natural phenomena (hail in Isaiah 28:2), social or political movements that gain momentum (2 Samuel 15:12), and men of war or resolute character (Amos 2:16). Job uses it to express divine omnipotence before which no one can stand. The meaning thus oscillates between raw strength and sovereign effectiveness.
H0533.portee: This word reminds the reader that true power is not merely physical, but is linked to firmness of character, lasting influence, and, above all, to the hand of God. Recognizing that God alone is "almighty" anchors the Christian faith in the certainty that nothing escapes His control and providence. For the believer, it is an invitation to place trust not in human or political forces, but in the One who holds all events in His hand.

sens: the top of a tree, its highest part
the summit of a mountain
figuratively, what is above, dominating
H0534.detail: 1. The summit is the highest part of a tree, where its branches end. In Isaiah 17:6, when the olive tree is shaken, only a few olives remain at the top of the summit, as it is the highest point of the foliage. 2. On a mountain, the summit refers to its peak, the highest point. Isaiah 17:9 mentions strong cities abandoned "on the summit of the mountains," meaning at the highest and most exposed places. 3. Figuratively, the summit represents what is dominant, what surpasses the rest — the image of the peak applied to what reigns or prevails.
H0534.origine: The Hebrew word אָמִיר (amir) likely comes from a root meaning "to elevate" or "to be high." It literally designates the highest point, the elevated part. The word belongs to the concrete and spatial vocabulary of ancient Hebrew, used to describe the visible heights of the natural world.
H0534.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Bible, both times in the prophet Isaiah (17:6 and 17:9). In these two passages, it describes abandoned places or bare spots: the rare olives that remain at the summit of the olive tree after shaking, and the strong cities left in ruins "on the summit of the mountains." The term thus emphasizes the desolation and solitude of the heights. Both uses illustrate the same meaning: the terminal and culminating point of a natural elevation.
H0534.portee: The summit evokes the fragility of what is elevated and exposed: the olives at the top are the most difficult to access and the most easily forgotten, while the cities on the mountain peaks become abandoned ruins. This image reminds the reader that even what seems strong and dominant can be forsaken.

sens: to become weak, lose vigor
to wither, fade (for a plant)
to be downcast, afflicted (morally or physically)
to be in desolation, sadness
H0535.detail:
1. The word primarily describes a physical weakening: something or someone that loses strength, vital energy. It is the image of vigor gradually exhausting, as in 1 Samuel 2:5 where she who had many children is "withered," meaning worn out, weakened.
2. It particularly applies to plants that wilt and lose their luster. In Isaiah 24:7, "the vine is withered," deprived of its greenness and productivity.
3. The word denotes the emotional and moral state of one who is overwhelmed, discouraged, without energy: a heart that weakens under the weight of sorrow. In Jeremiah 14:2, the cities of Judah are "desolate" and "sad" — it is the picture of ruin and mourning.
4. It expresses the general desolation of a land, a region struck by misfortune or God's judgment. In Hosea 4:3, the entire land is in mourning and all its inhabitants are "languishing": it is the image of a creation exhausted, drained of life.
H0535.origine: The Hebrew verb אָמַל comes from a root that expresses the fundamental idea of weakness and exhaustion. Its starting image is that of fatigue, of energy flowing away. The root is linked to contexts of illness, wear, and decay. The word belongs to the same semantic family as other Hebrew terms evoking sadness and weakening, and is used to describe both physical state and moral condition or that of creation.
H0535.emploi: This verb appears 14 times in the Old Testament, concentrated mainly in the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Hosea, Joel, Nahum) and in Lamentations. It describes situations of misfortune, judgment, or sadness. In prophecies, it often paints the desolation of the land struck by sin: withered vines, desolate land, languishing inhabitants. It can qualify the physical condition of a weakened person (1 Samuel 2:5) or the emotional state of mourning and despair (Lamentations 2:8). The word emphasizes less a passing moment than a persistent state of exhaustion and dejection.
H0535.portee: This word reminds us how sin, injustice, and distance from God produce weakness and death — not only in humans but in all creation. It shows that vitality, joy, and prosperity are gifts from God linked to obedience and trust in Him. For the Christian reader, it is an invitation to recognize how the lack of communion with God manifests as a kind of spiritual and moral exhaustion — and to seek, in Jesus, restoration and new life.

sens: Lacking physical strength or vigor
Weakened by suffering or illness
Having lost energy or the ability to act
H0536.detail:
1. The word describes a person devoid of physical strength, drained of natural vigor. In Psalm 6:3, the psalmist cries out to God, saying he is "without strength," unable to stand — his bones tremble, his body no longer responds.
2. It refers to the weakening caused by suffering or illness: the body becomes exhausted, energy flows away. The context of the Psalm shows a man afflicted in his flesh, at the end of his resources.
3. More broadly, it is the state of one who has lost all ability to act, all power: he can do nothing by himself and must rely on God's mercy.
H0536.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of being beaten down, annihilated, devoid of resilience. It evokes the image of a wilted plant or a body that collapses. The word belongs to the family of terms that describe weakness, exhaustion, and helplessness in the face of pain.
H0536.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 6:3. It is a prayer of distress: the psalmist, overwhelmed by suffering and illness, pleads with God to heal him. His lack of strength is not a shame, but an opportunity to confess his dependence on God. In this context of physical and spiritual crisis, the word paints a portrait of total vulnerability that calls for divine compassion.
H0536.portee: This word speaks to us at a time when we have exhausted our own resources and must turn to God. It validates the psalmist's experience of illness and weakness — something every believer can experience. It teaches us that confessing our fragility before God is not a failure, but the path to His healing and help.

sens: without physical strength, weak
unable to carry out a project
contemptible, worthy of derision
H0537.detail:
1. The word designates physical weakness: one who lacks vigor, strength to act. In Nehemiah 4:2, Sanballat mocks the Jews returned from exile by calling them "powerless" — he judges them too tired, too few to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem.
2. By extension, it refers to the inability to successfully carry out an endeavor, especially a difficult one. The word suggests not only personal weakness but insufficiency in the face of a task that exceeds available strength.
3. On a social and moral level, the powerless becomes an object of contempt. Sanballat uses this term to ridicule, to deny the Jews even the capacity to undertake: it is a sharp judgment, an attempt to discourage through denigration.
H0537.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of being soft, of sagging or disintegrating. The word belongs to the family of terms describing physical and moral weakness in biblical Hebrew. It is a rare word: it appears only once in the Bible.
H0537.emploi: This very rare word is used only once, in Nehemiah 4:2. It appears in the context of opposition to the rebuilding of the temple after the exile: Sanballat, the enemy governor, publicly mocks the project and the Jewish workers. The word expresses contempt and challenge in the face of what the enemy deems impossible to accomplish. This unique occurrence shows how the term serves a rhetoric of denigration and demotivation.
H0537.portee: For the Christian reader, this passage invites reflection on human judgment in the face of God's works. The Jews appeared powerless in Sanballat's eyes, but God supported them, and the wall was rebuilt. This teaches that the strength of the Lord is not measured by the opinions of the unbelievers or by outward appearances.

sens: City in the south of Judah
H0538.detail: Amam is a small city in the south of Judah, mentioned only once in the Bible during the enumeration of cities belonging to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:26). It was among the localities of the Negev, the desert region in the south of Palestine.
H0538.origine: The name Amam literally means "their mother" in Hebrew, which may evoke a source of water or a place of maternal importance for the inhabitants of the region. Although the etymology is clear, the precise reason for this name eludes us today.
H0538.emploi: Amam appears only once in Scripture, in Joshua 15:26, where it is listed among the cities belonging to the tribe of Judah after the conquest of Canaan. This brief mention shows that it was a real locality in the Negev, although its political or religious significance was minor.

sens: To trust in someone or something, to rely on their word or character
To recognize as true what is told to us, to accept a testimony
To be firm, solid, durable in existence or promise
To be faithful, trustworthy, reliable
To support, carry, nurture someone (concrete and rare sense)
H0539.detail:
1. To trust in someone or something is to rely on him, her, or it with assurance. It is the act of one who says "yes" to the word or promise of someone else, without doubt or hesitation. Abram did this in Genesis 15:6: he believed in the Lord's promise, and this trust was counted to him for righteousness. It is the opposite of doubt or rebellion.
2. To recognize as true is to accept a testimony or message as authentic. When Moses asks Pharaoh, "Will he be believed?" (Exodus 4:1), he is asking if Pharaoh will really believe this message. It is to believe news, to believe a story: to give credit to what is reported to us.
3. To be firm and durable: a promise "endures" forever (1 Chronicles 17:23), a reign is "established" forever (2 Samuel 7:16). This nuance comes from the concrete sense of "standing firm," "holding up." It is the solidity of a word or reality that holds strong.
4. To be faithful or trustworthy: the Lord is faithful in His promises, His works are "true," meaning confirmed and reliable (Psalms 111:7). It is also the character of one who can be trusted at their word. A "faithful" servant (1 Samuel 2:35) or a "reliable" friend (Proverbs 27:6) are people one can count on.
5. To support or carry someone: a nurturing father (what we translate as "foster-father") supports a child, carries them, raises them. This concrete image sheds light on the more figurative senses: to believe is also to be supported by trust in God.
H0539.origine: The Hebrew root אמן (aman) evokes the idea of solidity, stability, of what holds firm. It has given rise to the word אָמֵן (amen, "so be it"), which says "let it be so, let it hold." Other words from the same family speak of an artisan, a master (one who supports his craft), or a nurturing mother. The Greek of the Septuagint often translates this word with terms expressing faith, trust, certainty, showing that to believe is to accept the reality of what is told to us and to hold firmly to it.
H0539.emploi: This verb appears about a hundred times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the sense of "to believe" or "to have confidence." It appears as early as Genesis with Abram (Genesis 15:6), who believes in the Lord's promise, and throughout the history of Israel. The Hebrew people do not believe the message of the spies (Numbers 14:11) nor the voice of God at Sinai (Deuteronomy 1:32), while Moses, himself, doubts, and his unbelief prevents him from entering the promised land (Numbers 20:12). In the Psalms and Job, the word denotes trust in God or the absence of trust, doubt. In the historical or governmental realm, it means "to have charge of," "to prove trustworthy": a faithful servant is one in whom one can believe (1 Samuel 2:35, 3:20). The word also expresses the durability of a promise or word (it "endures," it is "established"). In the background, there is always the idea of solidity, firmness.
H0539.portee: This word at the heart of biblical faith reminds the reader that to believe is not a vague feeling, but a commitment: it is to recognize as true what God says and to rely on His faithfulness. Abram in Genesis 15 shows that this trust transforms a person: it places him righteous before God. Symmetrically, the unbelief or doubt of Israel in the desert or of Moses at Kadesh has lasting consequences. For the Christian, this word invites examination of whether their trust truly rests on the word of God, even when circumstances seem to say otherwise.

sens: To have confidence in someone or something, to rely on them
To be trustworthy, to be faithful and reliable
To be convinced of the truth or certainty of something
H0540.detail:
1. To have confidence in someone or something means to rely on them with all your heart: this is what Daniel does when he trusts in his God in the midst of danger (Daniel 6:23). It is a voluntary act of the will, saying "I lean on you".

2. To be trustworthy means to be faithful and reliable in what one says and does. Daniel was faithful: the officials of the kingdom found no fault or anything wrong in him (Daniel 6:4). It is a stable and reassuring character trait.

3. To be convinced of the certainty of something means to be sure that it is true and that it will come to pass. The interpretation of the king's dream is certain; it will indeed come to pass (Daniel 2:45).
H0540.origine: This Aramaic word is the confirmed form of the Hebrew word אָמַן (aman), which means "to be faithful" or "to be stable". It comes from a root that expresses the idea of support, stability, solid backing — like a mother supporting a child. The French word "amen" comes from this same Semitic root: to say "amen" is to say "yes, it is stable, it is true, I believe it."
H0540.emploi: This word appears three times in the book of Daniel, in Aramaic. It first describes the absolute certainty of a prophecy (Daniel 2:45: the king's dream and its interpretation are certain). Then, it characterizes Daniel's moral and professional faithfulness (Daniel 6:4), which nothing can tarnish. Finally, it expresses the personal act of trust: Daniel trusts in his God and emerges unscathed (Daniel 6:23). The word thus moves from the realm of objective certainty to the realm of personal relationship with God.
H0540.portee: This word invites the believer to imitate Daniel's trust: not a naive trust, but a trust rooted in the knowledge of who God is and His faithfulness. It brings peace in the heart during moments of danger or uncertainty. And it also calls every Christian to be faithful and trustworthy in their actions, just as Daniel was.

sens: To take the direction of the right, to turn to the right
Figuratively, to deviate from the path, to stray from the right way
H0541.detail:
1. The word denotes the physical action of directing oneself to the right or turning one's body in that direction. In Isaiah 30:21, the divine voice warns the people that they might "go to the right" — that is, deviate from the prescribed road, stray from the path they should follow.
2. Figuratively, "going to the right" (or "to the left") represents moving away from God's will, from the straight path He has marked. The image is that of a clearly defined road: one who leaves it to go to the right or left gets lost and risks falling into error.
H0541.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "right" or "right side". It is a variant of "yaman" (יָמַן), which has exactly the same meaning. In Hebrew, "right" is also related to "right-handed" and the idea of strength and dexterity: the right hand is the one that acts, that works. Here, the verb describes the action of choosing or taking that direction.
H0541.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 30:21. The prophecy features a voice crying behind the people to bring them back to the right path, at the moment they would be tempted to deviate. This context shows that the word fits into the biblical tradition of the path: righteousness means staying in the direction God indicates; straying to the right or left means getting lost and risking judgment.
H0541.portee: This passage reminds us that God does not abandon His people: He speaks to them, warns them, and brings them back to the right path. The explicit mention of the right and the left shows us that the Christian faith is not indifferent to choices; there is a right way, and turning away — even slightly — puts one in danger. It is a call to attentive obedience and vigilance.

sens: highly skilled worker who shapes a work with mastery
one who creates with skill and artistic ability
H0542.detail:
1. An artist is an expert worker, someone who masters their art to the point of transforming raw material into a beautiful and lasting creation. The word evokes the skillful hands of a master craftsman. In the Song of Solomon (7:2), the poet praises the elegant forms of a woman by comparing them to the carefully crafted work of an artist — as if each curve were shaped with consummate art.
2. Figuratively, it is one who creates with artistic intent, who does not merely produce but seeks beauty and harmony in what they do. It is the contrast between a mere maker and a true artist.
H0542.origine: The Hebrew word אָמָּן comes from a root that evokes firmness and solidity: the steady, diligent hand. It is one whose work is stable, rooted in long mastery of the craft. The primary notion is that of a sure hand, of proven experience that enables the creation of valuable works.
H0542.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Song of Solomon 7:2, where the poet uses the term to evoke the artistic perfection of feminine forms. Here, "artist" is not just a professional title: it is the comparison that elevates the subject to the beauty of a skillful creation, as if the praised human body were a work of art. The poetic and romantic context gives the word all its aesthetic weight.
H0542.portee: This word reminds us that well-done work, mastery, and art are realities worthy of respect in God's creation. It invites us to see beauty not as a superfluity, but as the fruit of artisanal excellence. For the believer, it also evokes that our hands, when they work with care and faithfulness, can reflect something of the Creator's work.

sens: Solemn affirmation of approval or adherence to what has just been said
Expression of a personal commitment to a word or a promise
Confirmation of the truthfulness of a word or a curse
Liturgical response of the people in blessings and curses
H0543.detail:
1. "Amen" is the exclamation by which the speaker or listener confirms and validates a solemn word. It is like saying: "May it be fulfilled" or "I confirm it." In Numbers 5:22, the woman suspected of adultery says "Amen! Amen!" to accept the effect of the curse or blessing; she commits herself with this double "Amen" to acknowledge the justice of what is to happen.
2. The word expresses a personal commitment to what is announced: the one who says "Amen" takes the word upon themselves and becomes responsible for it. When David responds "Amen" to Bathsheba (1 Kings 1:36), he ratifies his word given concerning Solomon.
3. "Amen" serves to confirm the truthfulness of a divine promise or the correctness of a curse. At each stanza of Deuteronomy 27, after the statement of a curse against the one who transgresses the law, "all the people shall say: Amen!" (vv. 15-26): the people attest that this curse is just and commit to respecting it.
4. In liturgy, "Amen" is the response of the assembled people to the word of God proclaimed by the priest or prophet. In Nehemiah 8:6, the people respond "Amen! Amen!" to Ezra's blessing, lifting their hands and bowing down: it is an act of bodily and spiritual adherence.
H0543.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be firm, to be stable, to lean on." It is found in the verb "amen" (to believe, to be certain) and in the noun "emet" (truth). "Amen" is thus the derived adjective or adverb: that which is stable, certain, truthful. This is why Isaiah 65:16 calls God "the God of Amen," meaning the God of truth and certainty: the one on whom one can absolutely rely.
H0543.emploi: The word "amen" appears 24 times in the Psalter and in the historical and prophetic Hebrew books. It is used in three ways: 1) In response to curses, particularly in the twelve curses of Deuteronomy 27 (vv. 15-26), where the people cry "Amen!" after each; 2) In ratification of a royal or prophetic word (1 Kings 1:36, when the people accept that Solomon is king); 3) At the end of doxologies and praises, especially in the Psalms (Psalms 41:14, 72:19, 89:53, 106:48), where "Amen" seals the blessing and commits the people to uphold it. It is a word that creates collective solidarity in the face of what is proclaimed.
H0543.portee: For the believer, "Amen" is never a mere formality. It is an act of faith: by saying "Amen" to a prayer, a promise, or a word from God, one commits oneself to God and before the community. It is to acknowledge that God is faithful ("the God of Amen") and to commit to living according to what has been heard. Through this word, the Bible shows us how to participate with all our being—mouth, heart, raised hands, prostrate body—in the word of God.

sens: Quality of one who keeps their promises and commitments
Reliable fulfillment of what has been decided or promised
Constancy and loyalty towards someone
H0544.detail:
1. Fidelity is the quality of one who keeps their word: the trust one can have in someone because they fulfill what they said they would do. In Isaiah 25:1, the "plans conceived in advance" have been "faithfully accomplished": God's plans have been realized with certainty, as promised.

2. This term also refers to the solidity and reliability of what is fulfilled: not only a promise, but its concrete realization, which does not fail. It is the assurance that what has been announced truly comes to pass.

3. More broadly, fidelity expresses lasting loyalty towards someone—especially towards God—a covenant that is not betrayed and that is honored day after day.
H0544.origine: The Hebrew word אֹמֶן comes from a root meaning "to be firm, sure, stable." It is related to the word אָמֵן ("amen"), which expresses affirmation and trust, and to the verb אָמַן ("to believe, to trust"). The starting image is that of something solid that one can lean on without fear of it giving way.
H0544.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 25:1. The prophet addresses God with praise for His plans and actions: he celebrates the fact that God keeps His promises and that what He has decided truly comes to pass. The context is one of trust in the Lord amidst the judgments and redemptions He accomplishes. Although rare, this word encapsulates a central conviction of Israel's faith: God is the one on whom one can absolutely rely.
H0544.portee: This word reminds the believer that God is not an arbitrary or fickle power, but someone who stands by His words. Divine promises are not empty words: they are fulfilled with a fidelity that never fails. It is a call to trust in the One who will never change and whose plans will come to fruition exactly as intended.

sens: The time during which someone is raised or cared for by a parent or guardian
The period of life when one depends on the education and care of another
Figuratively: the time of control or authority exercised over someone
H0545.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the time, the period during which a child is nourished, raised, and educated by a parent or caregiver. It is the time when one receives training and is entirely dependent on this responsible adult. In Esther 2:20, it refers to the time when Esther was under the authority and guidance of Mordecai, who had raised her after the death of her parents.
2. By extension, the word evokes the idea of a relationship of dependence and obedience: during this "period," the one being raised follows the orders and advice of the one who is raising them. Esther continued to obey Mordecai even after becoming queen, "as faithfully as during the time she was under his guardianship."
H0545.origine: This word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to nourish, to care for, to raise." It is linked to the idea of taking care of someone, providing for their material and moral needs as a parent does for their child. The word expresses the bond between the educator and the one receiving this training.
H0545.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Esther 2:20. It is used to describe the period during which Mordecai raised Esther after the death of her parents. The context shows that it is not merely a chronological period, but a time characterized by a relationship of education, care, and benevolent authority. Even once queen, Esther honors this relationship by continuing to follow Mordecai's advice.
H0545.portee: This word highlights the importance of education and training in a person's life. For Esther, this period of guardianship under Mordecai imparted wisdom and discipline, allowing her to grow in understanding. It is also a lesson on gratitude and honor owed to those who have raised and trained us, regardless of the changes in our lives.

sens: solemn affirmation of the truth of a thing
sincere acknowledgment of a fact
confirmation with strength and certainty
H0546.detail:
1. The word expresses a solemn affirmation: the one who pronounces it swears or strongly asserts the truth of what he says. When Abraham says to Abimelech, "Moreover, she is truly my sister," he wants to ensure that his interlocutor does not doubt this particular fact (Genesis 20:12).
2. It also marks sincere acknowledgment and admission of a fact that cannot be denied. When Achan says to Joshua, "It is true that I have sinned against the Lord," he confesses his guilt straightforwardly, admitting the reality of the evil he has committed (Joshua 7:20).
3. This word reinforces an affirmation and roots it in certainty: it is not a supposition, but an established and indisputable truth.
H0546.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root expressing solidity, firmness, and reliability ("amen" in Hebrew means "stable," "sure"). The adverb ômna thus carries the idea of an affirmation that stands firmly, which cannot be shaken. That is why this word is close to the one heard in "amen" — a word of confirmation and adherence to the truth.
H0546.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In both cases, it occurs in a moment of frankness: Abraham acknowledges a disturbing but true fact about the relationship with his wife, and Achan confesses his sin without evasion. It is a term that marks the moment when the truth imposes itself, whether it is uncomfortable or beneficial. The speaker suspends all ambiguity by stating his affirmation as certain and inevitable.
H0546.portee: This small word teaches the power of truthfulness: when one speaks truly, especially in difficult moments, one speaks with a firmness that nothing can contradict. For the Christian reader, it is an invitation to sincerity before God and others. Like Achan, confessing the truth, even painful, is accepting reality and opening oneself to repentance. It is also recognizing that the truth, spoken plainly, has its own authority.

sens: horizontal beam that supports the masonry above an opening
that which supports or holds something in place
H0547.detail:
1. The lintel is the beam or bar of wood, stone, or metal that extends horizontally above a door or window to support the wall that weighs upon it. It is an essential structural element: without it, the masonry would collapse. In 2 Kings 18:16, King Hezekiah removes the gold plates that covered the lintels of the temple, meaning those gold-decorated beams that formed the upper frame of the doors.
2. Figuratively, the word evokes the idea of support or backing: just as the lintel supports the structure of the building, that which supports or holds something symbolizes the strength that keeps it standing.
H0547.origine: The Hebrew word אֹמְנָה (omnah) comes from the root אמן (aman), which means "to be firm, to be stable, to be true." This root evokes the idea of solidity and reliability. The lintel embodies this solidity: it is a structure that remains firm and stable, that does not move. The same root has given rise to words like אָמֵן (amen, "so be it") and אֱמֶת (emet, "truth"), all related to the idea of what is solid, faithful, and enduring.
H0547.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Kings 18:16. It specifically refers to the lintels of the doors of the temple in Jerusalem, important architectural elements that King Hezekiah had covered with gold as a sign of wealth and piety toward the Lord. In his distress in the face of the Assyrian threat, he strips these precious ornaments to pay tribute to the king of Assyria. The technical term of building is used here in a serious historical and political context.
H0547.portee: This passage invites the reader to reflect on the true supports of life and faith. Hezekiah even abandons the ornaments of the temple — the house of God — to seek political security. It is a lesson on the danger of placing one's trust in material wealth or human alliances rather than in the help of the Lord. The lintel, a symbol of what supports and stabilizes, ironically becomes a silent witness to the spiritual instability of the moment.

sens: official or solemn agreement between two parties
assured and regular support or compensation
H0548.detail:
1. A covenant is an official and solemn agreement sealed between two parties, who commit themselves to one another. This is expressed in Nehemiah 9:38 when the people of Israel make a covenant with God and put it in writing: it is a serious commitment, ratified by the leaders, the Levites, and the priests by affixing their seal, as one would do for an important contract. The word evokes solidity and certainty: a covenant is something stable and durable, creating a mutual obligation.
2. The word can also refer to assured support, a fixed and certain compensation. In Nehemiah 11:23, each day the singers receive a regular salary, a support granted by order of the king: it is a guaranteed provision, a charge that rests on an established decision.
H0548.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of solidity, certainty, and stability. It is related to the image of something firm and assured, hence the meaning of covenant (an agreement that holds firm) and fixed support (a stable provision). This root is found in other Hebrew words of the same family that express trust and reliability.
H0548.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible: in Nehemiah 9:38, where it refers to the solemn covenant that Israel makes with God after the exile, and in Nehemiah 11:23, where it means the assured daily compensation for the singers of the temple. These two uses reflect the fundamental meaning of the term: something that is fixed, certain, and durable, whether it is an official pact or regular support. The context of Nehemiah shows the importance of this stability for the religious and administrative life of the people restored after the exile.
H0548.portee: This word reminds us that God does not act randomly, but establishes solid covenants and keeps His commitments. For the believer, it invites one to take seriously the agreements with God and to recognize that His faithfulness is certain and regular, like a salary that never fails. It is a word of assurance: God is someone one can count on.

sens: mountain range in the northeast of Lebanon, near the source of the Jordan
H0549G.detail: Amana is a mountain or mountain range located in the region of Lebanon, probably in the northeast, near the sources of the Jordan. It is mentioned in the Song of Solomon 4:8 as one of the majestic peaks from which the lover invites his beloved to contemplate the landscape ("Look from the top of Amana"). This name evokes a grand and rugged mountainous region, difficult to access, perhaps symbolizing wild and impressive beauty.
H0549G.origine: The name Amana literally means "support" or "that which supports," likely alluding to how this mountain range supports and encircles the surrounding lands. Its etymology reflects the image of a massive and stable mountain, serving as a foundation for the surrounding landscape.
H0549G.emploi: Amana appears only once in the Bible, in the Song of Solomon 4:8. It is listed among the famous mountains of the Levant (along with Senir and Hermon) that the lover contemplates, thus inscribing the landscape in a real and majestic geography of the ancient Near East.

sens: River of Syria that flows near Damascus
H0549H.detail: 1. Abana (or Amana) is a river in Syria that flowed down from the Anti-Lebanon mountains to the plain of Damascus. Its name literally means "support," probably because it nourishes and sustains the region. It is an important watercourse in ancient Syria.
H0549H.origine: The Hebrew word אֲמָנָה (Amana) means "support" or "sustenance." There is a variant אֲבָנָה (Abana), which is the more common name for the same river in the Bible. Both forms refer to the same watercourse that fed the lands around Damascus.
H0549H.emploi: Abana appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 5:12, when the Syrian general Naaman the Leper expresses his disappointment at the prophet Elisha's proposal. Naaman asks why he should wash in the Jordan when, he says, the rivers of Damascus (Abana and Parpar) are far more beautiful and pure than all the rivers of Israel. This geographical detail highlights Naaman's pride and the contrast between worldly wisdom (the apparent beauty of the Syrian river) and the simple faith required by God.
H0549H.portee: This passage reminds us that God's will is not tied to the appearance or prestige of the world. Naaman had to learn that obedience to God's prophet takes precedence over human logic. For the reader, it is an invitation not to rely on what seems great or beautiful in the eyes of men, but to trust the path that God indicates, even if it appears humble.

sens: eldest son of King David
prince of Judah during the united monarchy
H0550G.detail:
1. Amnon is the first son of David, born in Hebron to his relationship with Ahinoam of Jezreel (2 Samuel 3:2). He is therefore a royal prince, a potential heir to the throne of Israel.
2. Amnon lived during the time of the united monarchy, at the court of Jerusalem, among David's other sons and daughters. He is murdered by order of his half-brother Absalom (2 Samuel 13:28-29), who hated him for dishonoring their sister Tamar.
H0550G.origine: The name Amnon means "faithful" in Hebrew. He belongs to the royal family of David and is among the twelve sons born in Hebron before David was anointed king over all Israel.
H0550G.emploi: Amnon is mentioned 25 times in the Bible, primarily in 2 Samuel 13 and 1 Chronicles 3:1. The main account concerning him is in chapter 13 of 2 Samuel, where he is at the center of a family drama: he desires his half-sister Tamar, conspires with his friend Jonadab to lure her to his home, rapes her, and then rejects her with contempt. His crime triggers Absalom's vendetta, who kills him three years later during a sheep-shearing feast. Amnon embodies the firstborn son corrupted by royal power, given over to his unchecked desires.
H0550G.portee: The story of Amnon illustrates how royal power without fear of God leads to moral ruin and family destruction. It also shows the gravity of sexual sin in the eyes of God and the law of Israel, and how secret sin ultimately reveals itself and brings misfortune to the king's house.

sens: Son of Simon, of the tribe of Judah
H0550H.detail: Amnon is a man from the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:20. He is presented as the son of Simon and the brother of Rinnah, Ben-Hanan, and Thilon. Nothing else is known about him: the Bible simply gives us his name in a genealogy.
H0550H.origine: The name Amnon means "faithful" in Hebrew, derived from a root that expresses stability and reliability. It is an uncommon name in the Old Testament.
H0550H.emploi: Amnon appears only once in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 4:20, where he is listed among the sons of Simon. This mention historically situates this man during the time of the divided monarchy, but no details of his life or deeds are reported. It is a simple genealogical inclusion.

sens: Affirms the truth of a fact or statement
Marks agreement or reluctant admission
Affirms with strength certainty or evidence
H0551.detail:
1. This word affirms the absolute truth of a statement: what is said is real, in accordance with reality. In Ruth 3:12, Boaz says, "It is true that I have the right of redemption" — he acknowledges that it is an established fact, an undeniable reality. Similarly, King Hezekiah in 2 Kings 19:17 affirms before God: "It is true that the kings of Assyria have destroyed the nations" — he recognizes what has actually happened.
2. The word can also mark a forced admission or concession: one acknowledges something wrong, even reluctantly. In Job 19:4, Job says, "If indeed I have sinned" — he concedes the fact while wanting to show that he alone bears the responsibility. It is a "yes, it is true, but...".
3. Finally, it reinforces a negative assertion or a protest of innocence. In Job 34:12, it is categorically asserted, "No, indeed, God does not commit iniquity" — the word emphasizes the absolute certainty that God is just.
H0551.origine: This Hebrew adverb is formed from a root that means "to hold firmly, to be stable, true." It expresses what is solid, stable, established — what will not move, what is reliable. It is found in the word "amen" (אָמֵן), which also means "amen, it is true." The root evokes the idea of solidity and certainty.
H0551.emploi: The word appears nine times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the historical and poetic books (Ruth, 2 Kings, Job, Isaiah). It is used to affirm an undeniable fact (Ruth 3:12: a right of redemption), to acknowledge a historical reality (2 Kings 19:17: the Assyrian conquests), or to mark the admission of guilt or error (Job 19:4, 19:5). The context of Job often shows a speaker conceding a point while refuting what is inferred from it — it is a tactical concession. The adverb can also reinforce a solemn negation (Job 34:12: "No, indeed").
H0551.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of truth in biblical faith: what is true deserves to be acknowledged, even if it costs us. In the mouths of Boaz or the king, it is an expression of righteousness and honesty. For the believer, it invites us to imitate this frankness: to confess what is real, not to hide behind appearances, and to also recognize the absolute justice of God.

sens: Affirms the truth or reality of something
Reinforces a question to express astonishment or doubt
Marks a concession or solemn objection
H0552.detail:
1. The word expresses the affirmation of what is true or real. It is an insistence on the truth of a fact. In Genesis 18:13, Sarah exclaims: "Am I truly to have a child, now that I am old?" — she asks for confirmation of something that seems incredible to her, as she considers it impossible.
2. It reinforces a question to show astonishment, even doubt or incredulity. The question then carries all its weight: not only is a question posed, but it is posed with force, as if challenging the speaker to respond. This is the case when Solomon exclaims (1 Kings 8:27): "But will God truly dwell on the earth?" — this rhetorical question, reinforced by "truly," expresses the astonishment that an infinite God could dwell in a finite place.
3. Sometimes the word marks an objection or a concession: one acknowledges something as true while being astonished or contesting it. It is a "certainly, it is true, but..." that introduces an important correction or reservation.
H0552.origine: The Hebrew word אֻמְנָם (umnâm) comes from the root אמן (âman), which primarily means "to be stable, to be firm, to be true." It is the same root found in "amen" (אָמֵן), which solemnly confirms a truth. The adverb adds to this root a form that directs it toward affirmation: it says "it is firm, it is stable, it is true." The word thus expresses the solidity and certainty of an affirmation.
H0552.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is mainly used to pose rhetorical questions that express astonishment or doubt (Genesis 18:13: Sarah doubts that she can bear a child; 1 Kings 8:27 and 2 Chronicles 6:18: Solomon is astonished that God would dwell in a temple). It can also mark an objection or a concession (Numbers 22:37, Psalms 58:2). In all cases, the word reinforces the statement and gives it a solemnity: it is not a simple affirmation, it is a weighed, certified affirmation that almost challenges a response.
H0552.portee: This word teaches us to recognize true questions — those that, in interrogative form, hide an important affirmation or objection. When we read "Is it truly...?", we must listen not only to the question but also to the weight of certainty that carries it. For the believer, this means that doubting is not inherently bad: Abraham and Solomon express their doubts before God, and it is a form of honest dialogue with Him.

sens: To be strong, robust, powerful
To reinforce, give strength or courage to someone
To make firm, solid, unchangeable
To harden the heart, to make obstinate
To show courage, to determine, to persevere
H0553.detail:
1. To be strong, robust, powerful: this refers to the physical or moral strength of a person or thing. When the Lord tells Joshua that Rehoboam has "strengthened" the kingdom of Judah (2 Chronicles 11:17), it means he has made it strong and stable, capable of resisting. It is the solidity that lasts.

2. To reinforce, give strength or courage to someone: this is the action of communicating one's strength to another, making them capable and confident. The Lord tells Joshua: "Be strong and courageous, for you will bring the children of Israel into the land" (Deuteronomy 31:23) — He imparts the certainty and power to act.

3. To make firm, solid, unchangeable: this means to make something immovable, that does not waver. Job says: "I would strengthen you with my mouth" (Job 16:5), meaning he would reinforce his friends with his words, making them more stable in their trial.

4. To harden the heart, to make obstinate: this means to make a heart impervious to compassion or the will of God. When Pharaoh "hardened his heart" (Deuteronomy 2:30), he closed it and made it impervious to compassion.

5. To show courage, to determine, to persevere: this means for a person to take courage, to decide firmly and to hold fast. Naomi, seeing her daughter-in-law Ruth "determined" to go with her (Ruth 1:18), understands that she has made a firm decision and will not change her mind.
H0553.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of solidity and resistance — that which does not bend, that which holds firm. The same root gives rise to words like "hard," "strong," "solid." In Hebrew, this verb appears in several forms: it can describe the state (to be strong), the action on oneself (to strengthen oneself), or the action on another (to strengthen someone). It is a common word that takes on deep figurative meanings when it speaks of the heart or courage.
H0553.emploi: This verb appears 41 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) and in the Psalms. It is particularly frequent when the Lord commands His servants to take courage before a difficult mission: Moses commands it to Joshua (Deuteronomy 31:23), and the Lord Himself repeats it four times to Joshua (Joshua 1:6, 1:7, 1:9, 1:18). The word can also describe physical strength (Genesis 25:23: one people stronger than another) or the strengthening of an institution (2 Chronicles 11:17: to strengthen the kingdom). When applied to the heart, it often takes on a negative hue: hardening the heart of Pharaoh or Rehoboam means making it insensitive to justice. In the Psalms, it is a confident call: "Strengthen your hearts" (Psalms 27:14), addressed to those who hope in God.
H0553.portee: This word teaches the Christian reader that true strength comes from God and consists primarily of firmness of heart and moral courage, not carnal power. When God commands Joshua to strengthen himself, He does not promise him the absence of battle, but His presence. It is a constant call not to yield to fear or doubt, but to hold firm in faith. The hardening of the heart (like that of Pharaoh) warns that rejecting God leads to a progressive hardening: one distances oneself from His grace.

sens: Horse of red or reddish color
Spotted or piebald horse, with red spots
H0554.detail:
1. The word designates a horse of red or reddish color, a dark and strong hue. It is the color observed in the horses of the chariot seen by the prophet Zechariah in his vision of the heavenly horses (Zechariah 6:3).
2. It can also describe a horse with red spots or a piebald coat, a mix of colors. In Zechariah's vision, these red horses come down from heaven and traverse the earth at the command of the angel (Zechariah 6:7).
H0554.origine: The Hebrew word אָמֹץ comes from a root that evokes strength and vigor. The initial meaning of "strong" has extended to the description of horses of strong or striking color — red or spotted — probably because this dark and intense color recalls strength. The word appears only in Zechariah, in the context of the prophet's visions.
H0554.emploi: This word appears only twice in Zechariah 6, in the vision of the horses of the heavenly chariots. Zechariah sees a chariot with four horses of different colors: white, red (or red-spotted), and black. The red horses go out and traverse the earth — they are the messengers of divine will. The word emphasizes their remarkable and majestic character among the heavenly horses.
H0554.portee: This vision of the red horses traversing the earth symbolizes God's vigilance and action as He observes and governs the world. For the believer, it serves as a reminder that the Lord sees all that happens on earth and acts according to His plans, even when His presence remains invisible.

sens: Power, physical or moral strength
Courage, firmness of spirit in trial
Ability to persevere despite obstacles
H0555.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes strength, power, solidity: the capacity of a being to hold firm, to resist. It conveys the idea of solidity and stability.
2. It also evokes courage and moral firmness — this inner strength that allows one not to waver in the face of adversity or temptation. In Job 17:9, the righteous "grows stronger and stronger": he draws from within a constant strength to remain faithful to his path, even when everything seems to abandon him.
3. Finally, the word emphasizes perseverance: not a strength that bursts forth only once, but a solidity that asserts itself each day, growing with time and trial.
H0555.origine: The Hebrew root expresses the idea of "to squeeze," "to hold firmly," from which the sense of strength and solidity naturally derives. It is a simple, concrete word that first paints a physical reality before extending to the moral domain. The corresponding verb means "to strengthen" or "to be strong."
H0555.emploi: The word is rare in the Hebrew Bible. It appears in the Segond translations only in Job 17:9, where it describes the growing firmness of the righteous in his conduct despite his sufferings. This context shows that the strength in question is not muscular, but moral and spiritual: it is the ability to remain stable, upright, and faithful when going through trials.
H0555.portee: This word reminds the believer that true strength is not found in wealth or human power, but in moral firmness and faithfulness to God. For those who suffer, it assures that God grants the righteous a strength that grows, that strengthens each day: an inner power that does not wear out.

sens: physical or moral power
solidity and firmness in action
ability to resist or hold firm
H0556.detail:
1. Strength denotes physical or moral power — the ability to act with vigor. In Zechariah 12:5, the leaders of Judah recognize that the inhabitants of Jerusalem are their strength, meaning their support, the one they can rely on to hold firm against the enemy.
2. This word evokes solidity and firmness: what allows one to stand, to resist, not to bend. It is a quality of one who has the necessary resources to face difficulties.
3. Strength can also refer to the ability to hold firm morally, not to weaken in trial — a form of courage or determination that comes from the heart.
H0556.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of solidity and firmness. It belongs to the family of words that describe what is hard, resistant, capable of bearing weight. It is a concrete term at first — the strength of the body or of stone — which extends to the figurative sense to speak of moral strength or the support one derives from an ally.
H0556.emploi: This word appears only once in the preserved Hebrew biblical text, in Zechariah 12:5. In this passage, the leaders of Judah speak in their hearts and declare that the inhabitants of Jerusalem — a city, a people — are their strength. This usage shows how one calls "strength" the one or those on whom one relies, in whom one has confidence to face adversity. The prophetic context reinforces the idea: it is the strength that the Lord gives them through His help.
H0556.portee: This word reminds the believer that true strength does not primarily come from our own power, but from those with whom we are united — and ultimately from the Lord. When Judah recognizes that Jerusalem is his strength, it is an act of faith: he confesses his dependence on what God has established and preserved. For us, this invites us to seek our strength not in ourselves, but in the Lord and in the fellowship He gives us.

sens: Levite of the divided monarchy period
H0557G.detail: Amtsi is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 6:46. He is presented as the son of Bani and the father of Hilkiah. His name means "my strength" or "my power." He lived during the divided monarchy in Israel and was part of the Levitical lineage that served the temple.
H0557G.origine: The name Amtsi comes from the Hebrew root meaning "strength" or "power," with the possessive suffix "my." He belongs to the family of Levites, the descendants of Levi charged with religious service in Israel.
H0557G.emploi: Amtsi appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 6:46, in a genealogy of the Levites. He is cited in the succession of Bani and Hilkiah, being part of the ancestors of the Levites who served after the exile to Babylon. This genealogical mention shows his importance in the continuity of the Levitical priestly lineage.

sens: Levite of the post-exilic return period
Ancestor of a family of priests returned from captivity
H0557H.detail: 1. Amtsi is a Levite mentioned in the genealogies of the return from exile, that is, after the Jews were able to return from Babylon. His name literally means "my strength" in Hebrew. 2. He is the ancestor of a priestly lineage: he is the father of Pelaiah and the grandfather of Adaiah, all three listed among the priests and Levites who returned to serve in the restored temple of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 11:12). This genealogy shows how the religious life of Israel was rebuilt after the exile.
H0557H.origine: The name Amtsi means "my strength" (composed of two Hebrew elements: "oz" = strength and the possessive "-i" = my). This name is borne in the Levitical lineage, highlighting the spiritual strength of this family in the service of the temple. The name appears unique in the preserved biblical texts.
H0557H.emploi: Amtsi is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:12, in a genealogical register listing the priests and Levites returned from captivity to Jerusalem. He appears in a long chain of generations: son of Zechariah and father of Pelaiah. This list shows how the priestly families restored the temple worship after the return from Babylonian exile.

sens: King of Judah, son of Joash
H0558G.detail: Amatsia is a king of Judah who reigned during the period known as the divided monarchy, between the northern kingdom (Israel) and the southern kingdom (Judah). He is the son of King Joash and the father of Uzziah (also called Azariah). His story occupies an important place in the Books of Kings and Chronicles, particularly chapters 14 and 25 of 2 Chronicles, which recount his military exploits and failures.
H0558G.origine: The name Amatsia means "Jehovah is powerful" or "Jehovah is strength." It is composed of two elements: "Amat" which evokes divine power or strength, and "Yah," a shortened form of Jehovah. This theophoric name (containing the name of God) expresses the trust that parents placed in divine protection over their son.
H0558G.emploi: Amatsia is mentioned 34 times in the Bible, mainly in 2 Kings 14-15 and 2 Chronicles 24-26. The account in 2 Kings 12:21 presents him as succeeding his father Joash. His most notable acts are reported in 2 Chronicles 25: he gathers an army, wins a victory against Edom in the Valley of Salt by defeating ten thousand men (2 Chronicles 25:11), but makes the mistake of provoking King Joash of Israel to battle (2 Chronicles 25:18-20), which costs him his defeat and capture at Beth-Shemesh (2 Kings 14:11-12). Upon his death, his son Azariah, aged sixteen, succeeds him (2 Kings 14:21).
H0558G.portee: The story of Amatsia illustrates how military success and human courage are insufficient without obedience to God. Although he won a spectacular victory against Edom, his pride and refusal to heed warnings (2 Chronicles 25:15-16) led him to defeat against Israel. His journey teaches the believer that true strength comes from God alone, and that humility and obedience are better than displays of power.

sens: Man of the tribe of Simeon during the time of the divided monarchy
H0558H.detail: 1. Amatsia is a man belonging to the tribe of Simeon, mentioned only once in the Bible at a time when Israel was divided into two kingdoms (Northern Kingdom and Southern Kingdom). He appears in a genealogy of the descendants of Simeon (1 Chronicles 4:34).
H0558H.origine: The name Amatsia means "Yahweh (God) is powerful." It comes from the combination of two Hebrew roots: "Amat" (strength, power) and the divine name "Yah." It is a theophoric name, like many Hebrew names, which expresses faith in divine power. Other biblical characters bear this name, including a king of Judah and a priest of Bethel.
H0558H.emploi: Amatsia is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:34, where he appears in a genealogical list of the descendants of Simeon. The text indicates that he is the father of Joscha. This very brief and purely genealogical mention allows us to know that such a man existed in the tribe of Simeon, but it gives us no details about his life or actions.

sens: Levite of the tribe of Levi
Singer in the service of the tabernacle
H0558I.detail:
1. Amatsia is a Levite, meaning a descendant of the tribe of Levi, chosen by God to serve in the tabernacle. He appears in the genealogy of the temple servants during the time of King David (1 Chronicles 6:45).
2. His role was that of a singer in the service of the tabernacle—one of the sacred functions that the Levites performed to accompany the public worship of Israel through music and songs.
H0558I.origine: The name Amatsia means "Jehovah is powerful." It is formed from two parts: "Ama" which refers to power or strength, and "Jah" which designates the God of the covenant, Yahweh. This name expresses the trust that parents placed in God's power. The Bible mentions several men bearing this name at different times, but this one is a Levite during the time of David.
H0558I.emploi: Amatsia is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 6:45, in a long genealogical list of Levites assigned to the functions of singers of the tabernacle. He is presented as the son of Hilkijah and the father of Hashabiah, thus recording his lineage in the Levitical priestly function. This isolated mention shows the importance that the Bible places on preserving the record of the Levitical musicians who enriched the temple worship.

sens: Priest of Bethel
Adversary of the prophet Amos
H0558J.detail: 1. Amatsia is a priest attached to the royal sanctuary of Bethel, located in the northern kingdom of Israel, where a rival worship was established against the temple of Jerusalem. 2. He appears in the account of the book of Amos as one who opposes the message of the prophet: he denounces him to King Jeroboam II (Amos 7:10), claiming that Amos is conspiring against the state, and then he orders the prophet to leave (Amos 7:12). Amos responds clearly to him: he is not a professional prophet, but a simple shepherd and sycamore farmer whom God has called to deliver His message (Amos 7:14).
H0558J.origine: The name means "Jehovah is powerful" in Hebrew: it combines the notion of divine strength with the name of the God of Israel. It is a name borne by several figures in the Old Testament, but the usages provided refer only to the priest of Bethel contemporary with Amos.
H0558J.emploi: Amatsia appears three times in the account of Amos 7:10-14, where he plays the role of the religious and political opponent to the prophet. As a priest of the royal sanctuary, he holds religious authority and seeks to protect the established order by denouncing one who challenges the official worship. His conflict with Amos reveals the tension between authentic prophecy and institutional religion in the northern kingdom at that time.
H0558J.portee: This character illustrates how established religious structures can become deaf to the voice of God. Amatsia prefers to defend his status and system rather than listen to the message of the prophet. For the Christian reader, Amatsia reminds us that true spiritual authority does not come from titles or position, but from God's calling, as shown by Amos's humble response.

sens: To express words, to emit an articulated voice
To respond to someone, to engage in dialogue
To command, to order something
To think inwardly, to conceive in one's heart
To promise, to commit by word
H0559.detail:
1. To express words, to emit an articulated voice: this is the simplest and most common meaning. God "said" at creation: "Let there be light!" (Genesis 1:3), putting into words what He wants to bring about. Every act of speech, from the most ordinary to the most solemn, is expressed this way.

2. To respond to someone, to engage in dialogue: this means to speak in reaction to a question or an appeal. Samson "responds" to the men of Judah who question him about his actions (Judges 15:11); the exchange implies a word that bounces off another. This meaning shows that "to say" is not isolated but relational.

3. To command, to order something: the word becomes directive, creating an obligation. Moses "said" to Pharaoh orders from the Lord (Exodus 32:11 and context); the father "says" to his son why he acts this way, establishing a norm (1 Kings 1:6). It is to speak with authority.

4. To think inwardly, to conceive in one's heart: "to say in one's heart" means to form a thought, a secret resolution. The word exists first internally before coming out of the mouth: it is to conceive and deliberate.

5. To promise, to commit by word: to say becomes an act that binds the speaker. The Lord "said" to Abraham a promise that engages His honor and power (Genesis 12:1, 15:1-18); a divine word is never in vain.
H0559.origine: The Hebrew verb אָמַר (amar) is a very ancient Semitic root, common to Arabic (qāla) and Aramaic (אֲמַר, amar). The original image is that of making oneself heard, producing an articulated sound. The root has no etymological link to a specific gesture or object: it points directly to the act of speech itself, one of the most essential realities of human and divine communication. Words from the same family include אִמְרָה (imra, "word"), formed from the same root.
H0559.emploi: The verb "to say" (אָמַר) is the most frequently used Hebrew verb in the Bible with 4,339 documented uses. It dominates from Genesis, where God creates by His word: "God said: Let there be light!" (Genesis 1:3, 6, 9, etc.). Throughout the biblical narrative, it serves to report the direct speech of God, prophets, patriarchs, and all actors. Moses "said" to God his intercessions (Exodus 32:11); men speak to each other using this verb. Its primary meaning remains simple verbal expression, but it also encompasses command (Nehemiah 13:17: reprimanding by saying), promise (Genesis 12:1-2), and even silent thought ("to say in one's heart"). No other Hebrew verb surpasses it for reporting speech; it is the fundamental verb of biblical dialogue.
H0559.portee: Understanding that "to say" is the quintessential act of relationship between God and humanity. God creates and governs by His word; man responds, asks, and confides also through speech. This verb shows that the Bible never separates thought from the heart and expression: "to say" is to engage, to create a reality, to establish a covenant. For the Christian reader, this sheds light on why Jesus is called "the Word": in Him, the word of God takes flesh and fulfills what it promises. Honoring the word is to honor God.

sens: Express in words, make one's voice heard
Speak to someone, engage in dialogue
Command, order
Report, recount
Relate a dream or vision
H0560.detail:
1. The basic meaning: to express something in words. It is simply to open one's mouth and speak. In Daniel 3:25, the king "said": "I see four men unbound" — he states aloud what he sees.

2. To speak to someone, to have an exchange. Often it involves addressing a specific person to communicate with them. In Ezra 5:3, the governors "spoke" to the Jews to ask who had authorized them to build.

3. To command, to give an order. The word takes on a nuance of authority: the one who "says" exercises power and expects obedience. In Daniel 2:46, the king "commanded" that sacrifices be offered to Daniel.

4. To report, to communicate information, often in a formal or official manner. It is to convey a message from one person to another. In Daniel 2:9, the king threatens: "If you do not make known to me the dream, you want to 'say' lies to me."

5. To relate, to recount a dream or vision, which is very common in the book of Daniel. In Daniel 7:1-2, Daniel "said": "I looked during my night vision..."
H0560.origine: This Aramaic word is equivalent to the Hebrew "amar" (אָמַר), the most common Hebrew verb for saying. The word comes from a very ancient root that expresses the action of pronouncing, emitting sounds with intention. Most Semitic verbs of speech — whether Hebrew, Aramaic, or Arabic — share this root, which shows its antiquity and fundamental importance in Middle Eastern languages. It is a simple and direct word, without particular connotation of secrecy or hidden intention.
H0560.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the Aramaic Bible: about 65 occurrences. It appears mainly in the Aramaic portions of Daniel (chapters 2 to 7) and Ezra (chapters 4 to 6). In these books, it introduces dialogues, solemn statements, and narratives. In Ezra, it reports official letters and exchanges between Persian authorities and the Jews. In Daniel, it frames the visions, the speeches of King Nebuchadnezzar, the responses of the young Hebrews, and the interpretation of dreams. The meaning slightly evolves according to the context: "say" when it is a simple statement, "speak" when it is a dialogue, "order" when authority reigns, "relate" when recounting a dream or vision. But the core remains always the expression through speech.
H0560.portee: This humble verb reminds the reader that speech is the instrument by which things are made known and realized. In Daniel and Ezra, God speaks through His messengers, and His words accomplish His will. It is also a word that shows how human beings — kings, wise men, young people — enter into conversation, debate, and confrontation. For the believer, it emphasizes the importance of listening carefully to what is said and recognizing where true wisdom comes from.

sens: What comes out of the mouth, expressed in words
Extended discourse, development of a thought
Order given, commandment
Promise or commitment spoken
Subject of conversation
H0561.detail:
1. The word is primarily a vocal statement, what is expressed in words: in Genesis 49:21, Naphtali "utters beautiful words," meaning he pronounces gracious words.
2. It also refers to a broader discourse, a series of developed statements: Job 6:26 contrasts the "words of a desperate man" with thoughtless remarks, and Proverbs 4:20 invites to be "attentive to my words" to listen to a sustained teaching.
3. The word can be an order or directive given: in Deuteronomy 32:1, Moses invites the earth to listen to his words, and in Joshua 24:27, the stone will serve as a witness against Israel if the people transgress the word of the Lord.
4. It can also express a commitment or promise: Psalm 138:4 mentions how kings praise "the word" of the Lord, referring to His commitments.
5. Finally, it can simply refer to a subject of conversation or a matter being discussed (Proverbs 19:7, where one refuses to listen to the words of the poor).
H0561.origine: The Hebrew word אֵמֶר comes from a root meaning "to say, to speak." It is related to other Hebrew forms of the verb to say. In Hebrew, the word is never just a noise: it has weight, it engages the one who pronounces it, it creates bonds. This is why the word can refer interchangeably to an ordinary word and a divine commandment, both of which create a reality.
H0561.emploi: The word אֵמֶר appears 47 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Proverbs, Psalms, and the speeches of Job. It is generally translated as "word" in English. In wisdom literature (Proverbs and Job), it refers to the words of the one who teaches or speaks: the wise invite others to listen to their words, and Job defends his words against his accusers. In the Psalms, it can be the word of the Lord or that of the psalmist who prays. Words are always the subject of listening, judgment, and attention: they are never neutral.
H0561.portee: For the Christian reader, this vocabulary entry shows that the word has power: it engages. It creates, it binds, it resonates beyond the moment it is spoken. By listening to the words of God, one receives not only information but an order that transforms. Conversely, no one can speak without responsibility: every word will be weighed.

sens: Vocal statement, what is said
Discourse, language considered in its form
Message carrying intention or authority
Promise or commitment expressed
Decision or directive
Rumor or what is reported
H0562.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to anything that comes out of the mouth: a spoken word, a statement. In Habakkuk 3:9, the "arrows of Your word" evoke words as arrows shot by God, striking and effective.
2. It can also refer to language itself, the manner of expression. Psalms 19:4 speaks of a "language" that does not need sound to be heard: it is the silent discourse of creation.
3. A word often carries authority, a force of command or promise. Psalms 77:9 asks if the "word" of God can be annulled: this word then designates divine commitment, His expressed faithfulness.
4. The word can also express a resolution, a deliberate statement to which one adheres. In Job 22:28, "your resolutions" (lit. your words) will succeed: it is your determined word that will be accomplished.
5. It sometimes designates what is reported or transmitted, a message. Psalms 68:12 states that the Lord "said a word" and immediately the messengers announce victory.
6. In Psalms 19:3, "one day tells another day" speaks of what one day transmits to the next: it is the silent teaching, the word without voice.
H0562.origine: This word comes from a Hebrew root meaning fundamentally "to say." It is related to other Hebrew words designating speech and statement. Its primordial image is that of the statement that comes out of the mouth, the very act of speaking. The notion gradually enriches: from simple vocal speech to a message carrying intention, to a binding promise, to an effective order.
H0562.emploi: This word appears six times in the provided passages, mainly in the Psalms and the prophets. In Habakkuk and Psalms 68, it designates the powerful word of God that commands and accomplishes. In Psalms 77, it evokes divine commitment or promise, by which God binds Himself. In Job 22, it corresponds to personal resolution that finds its fulfillment. In Psalms 19, it takes on a broader sense of communication or transmission, including the silent word of creation. The usage varies between concrete statement and the message or promise of eternal significance.
H0562.portee: This word reminds us that God's word is never empty: it creates, it engages, it is fulfilled. For the believer, it emphasizes that every word of God is operative and reliable, and one should not fear that it will be annulled. It also teaches us that our own words and resolutions carry weight and must be spoken with sincerity, since we are created in the image of a God whose word creates.

sens: Young male sheep intended for sacrifice
Animal offered in the rituals of the Jerusalem temple
Atoning victim for sins
H0563.detail:
1. The lamb is a young male sheep, without blemish, raised to be sacrificed. It is the most common animal for burnt offerings and sacrifices at the temple. In Ezra 6:17, during the dedication of the temple, four hundred lambs are offered along with bulls and rams: it is an animal of lesser value than the bull, but numerous and therefore accessible for large offerings.
2. Lambs are regularly provided to the temple for daily burnt offerings. Ezra 6:9 specifies that "the lambs" are part of the necessary items delivered to the priests day after day: they constitute the regular and ordinary offering, more frequent than that of bulls or rams.
3. The lamb can represent an atoning victim, an animal whose blood purifies the people from their sins. Although this meaning is not explicitly developed in these three passages from the book of Ezra, the lamb throughout the Bible carries this dimension of sacrifice for sin.
H0563.origine: The Hebrew word אִמַּר (immar) specifically refers to a young ram or male lamb. It comes from an Aramaic-Hebrew root and belongs to the vocabulary of temple sacrifices. This word appears mainly in the contexts of restoring worship after the exile (the book of Ezra), when it is necessary to specify the animals to be offered.
H0563.emploi: The word appears three times in the Bible, all in the book of Ezra (chapters 6 and 7), a text that recounts the restoration of the temple in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile.
