In each case, it is used to determine the quantities of lambs to be purchased or delivered for the temple sacrifices: it is a precise administrative and liturgical term. In Ezra 6:9, the lambs are listed among the daily provisions for worship; in 6:17 and 7:17, they appear in the lists of animals intended for solemn dedication offerings.
H0563.portee: For the believer, the lamb reminds us that sin requires a bloody sacrifice, a price paid to God. In the Old Testament, this endless succession of lambs signified the insufficiency of the old worship. The Bible teaches that Jesus is "the Lamb of God" who takes away the sin of the world: a single unblemished lamb, offered once for all, replaces all those lambs of the temple.

sens: Levite from the tribe of Levi, ancestor of priests during the Exile and the Return
Man whose name means 'he has spoken'
H0564G.detail:
1. Immer is a Levitical ancestor whose name appears in the priestly genealogies of the return from Babylon. He is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 9:12 as the ancestor of Meshillemoth, and in Nehemiah 11:13 as the ancestor of Amashsai. These genealogical lists from the time of Nehemiah show that several priests claimed descent from him, indicating his importance in the Levitical priesthood.
2. His Hebrew name literally means "he has spoken" or "the one who speaks," an image that may evoke an ancestor known for his speech or prophetic authority, although the Bible does not provide further details about his personality or deeds.
H0564G.origine: The name Immer comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to speak" or "to say." This type of theophoric name (containing a reference to God) was common in Israel to honor a divine intervention. The name suggests that this ancestor was associated with a memorable divine word at his birth or through his actions.
H0564G.emploi: Immer appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, in the two main genealogical documents of the return from Exile: 1 Chronicles 9:12 and Nehemiah 11:13. In these two verses, he is cited as an indirect ancestor of priests who resumed service at the Temple after the return from Babylonian captivity. These mentions show that his priestly line survived the Exile and that his descendants played an active role in the restoration of worship in Jerusalem. The fact that he is named in these two independent lists confirms the historical importance of this Levitical family.
H0564G.portee: The memory of Immer in the priestly genealogy reminds us of God's faithfulness to his descendants and his promise to preserve a remnant capable of serving in the restored Temple after the Exile. For the Christian reader, this illustrates how God maintains his line of succession and honors those who are dedicated to him, even through trials and captivities.

sens: priest during the time of King David
priest during the time of the prophet Jeremiah
father of the priest Zadok
ancestor of a line of priests
H0564H.detail:
1. Immer is first a priest during the time of King David (1 Chronicles 24:14). His name appears in the list of the heads of priestly families, where he receives the fifteenth course of service at the Temple.
2. Immer also appears as a family name borne by priests during the time of Jeremiah (Jeremiah 20:1: Pashhur, son of Immer, was a priest and chief inspector of the Temple).
3. Immer is mentioned as the father of the priest Zadok, an important figure in the priesthood of Israel.
4. The descendants of Immer continued: after the Babylonian exile, his descendants returned in large numbers (Ezra 2:37 and Nehemiah 7:40 report that one thousand fifty-two sons of Immer returned to Jerusalem), showing that he was the head of a large family of priests.
H0564H.origine: The name Immer means "he has said" in Hebrew, formed from the root that expresses speech. This name was borne by several members of the priesthood of Israel over generations, testifying to its importance in the service of the Temple.
H0564H.emploi: Immer appears five times in Scripture, primarily as the name of a priestly lineage. He is first mentioned in 1 Chronicles 24 as one of the heads of priestly families during the time of David. His role is confirmed during the return from exile with his many descendants (Ezra 2:37; Nehemiah 7:40). He is also encountered as the father of Pashhur in Jeremiah 20:1, a priest who opposed the prophet Jeremiah. Two of his sons also appear in the list of those who had taken foreign wives (Ezra 10:20). Immer represents a stable and influential priestly lineage throughout Israel's history.

sens: Place or region in Israel from which some exiles returned
H0564I.detail: 1. Immer is a place or region mentioned as a starting point for some Israelites returning from exile. During the return of the Babylonian captives, families from four localities — Thel-Melah, Thel-Harsha, Kerub-Addan, and Immer — could not prove their Israelite ancestry, complicating their reintegration into the community (Nehemiah 7:61).
H0564I.origine: The name literally means "he has said" in Hebrew, but its application to this place indicates an ancient connection with the geography of Israel. It is likely a location or region whose name was preserved in the memory of the exiles, although its precise location today is uncertain.
H0564I.emploi: Immer appears twice in the Bible, only in the lists of return from captivity: once in Ezra 2:59 under the form "Kerub-Addan" and once in Nehemiah 7:61 under the name "Immer." These two parallel passages describe the same historical event — the return of the exiles from Babylon — and mention this place among the localities whose inhabitants had lost the evidence of their Israelite genealogy.

sens: priest during the time of David and Jeremiah
father of the priest Zadok
H0564J.detail:
1. Immer is a priest mentioned during the reign of King David and the prophet Jeremiah. His name appears in the records of the priestly families of Israel, those who served in the temple.
2. Immer is the father of Zadok, a priest who participated in the reconstruction of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. He is seen working on the city's walls, carrying out restoration work in front of his own house (Nehemiah 3:29).
H0564J.origine: The name Immer means "he has spoken" in Hebrew, derived from the root that expresses speech. It is a theophoric name, meaning a name that includes the idea of a divine action or a relationship with God. Several men bore this name in the Israelite priestly context.
H0564J.emploi: Immer designates a priest of the people of Israel about whom little is known, but who is part of an important priestly lineage. His son Zadok followed the same path: he was also a priest and was among those who rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem after the return from exile (Nehemiah 3:29). This Zadok is clearly identified as the "son of Immer," which shows that priestly lineage and the honor of fathers were passed down in these families devoted to temple service.

sens: Spoken utterance, what comes out of the mouth
Word of God, divine command or promise
Promise, solemn commitment
Speech, teaching
Hearing, what is heard
H0565A.detail:
1. It is primarily a word, something that is said and expressed: in Genesis 4:23, Lamech cries out to his wives, "Listen to my word!" — it is his voice, his statements that come out of his mouth.
2. When it is the word of God, it is never empty: it is a command (what God ordains) or a promise (what God commits to do). In Psalms 119:41, the psalmist pleads: "Let your mercy come upon me, Your salvation according to Your promise!" — he relies on what God has said He would do.
3. A promise, in particular, is a commitment that cannot be withdrawn: in Psalms 119:82, the psalmist waits for his comfort "according to Your promise" — he knows that God will keep His word.
4. It is also a discourse, a word addressed that one listens to: "Listen to my word!" means "Listen to what I have to say to you." 
5. Sometimes, it is simply what one hears, what reaches the ear: a hearing, a received message.
H0565A.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root אמר (amar), which means "to say." An imrah is therefore what is said, the statement or utterance that comes from speech. In Hebrew, the word is often used for solemn, engaging, or divine words, those that carry weight and authority.
H0565A.emploi: The word appears 34 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the Psalms and the prophetic books. It designates sometimes an ordinary word (Genesis 4:23: the word of Lamech), but much more often the word of God. In Psalms 119, the psalmist repeatedly refers to "Your word," "Your promise": he cherishes it (verse 140: "Your word is entirely tested"), meditates on it (119:11), keeps it (119:38), finds comfort in it (119:50). This divine word is reliable, tested, it transforms (105:19: the word of the Lord tested Joseph). The translation varies: "word" when it is the statement itself, "promise" when emphasizing the commitment it contains.
H0565A.portee: For the believer, this word of God is not a passing noise: it is a command that demands obedience, a promise on which one can fully rely. Psalm 119 shows that one can live by this word, cherish it as one cherishes a treasure, draw strength and comfort from it. It is "entirely tested" — one can trust it.

sens: Word of threat or judgment pronounced by God
Firm and unchangeable decision of God
H0565B.detail:
1. The word designates a word of threat or judgment that God has pronounced — a word that expresses His anger and intention to punish. In Lamentations 2:17, the Lord "has fulfilled the word that He had long ago determined": it is His word of destruction against Jerusalem, which He had kept in His heart and which He ultimately executed at the fall of the city.
2. This word is not a mere threat that might not come to pass: it is a definitive and unchangeable decision of God. It is "determined," meaning established once and for all, and it will certainly be fulfilled. It is the word of a God whose judgment is just and whose word cannot fail.
H0565B.origine: The Hebrew word אֶמְרָה (imrah) comes from the root אמר (amar), which means "to say" or "to speak." It designates primarily a spoken word, then more specifically an authoritative word, a declaration that has the force of law or judgment. In the context of divine judgment, it takes on the color of a threat or an inexorable divine sentence.
H0565B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Lamentations 2:17. It is used to describe the word of judgment that God had pronounced against Jerusalem and which was realized during its destruction by the Babylonians in 586 B.C. This word was not new at the time of destruction: it had been "long ago determined" by God, showing that His judgment was thoughtful, just, and irrevocable. The unique use of the word underscores the importance and solemnity of this divine judgment.
H0565B.portee: This word reminds the reader that God does not pronounce His threats lightly: His words of judgment are serious, thoughtful, and certain to be fulfilled. For the people of God in exile, this could be painful — recognizing that their destruction was justified and predetermined — but it was also an invitation to repentance and trust in a God whose word is reliable.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the time of exile and return
H0566G.detail: Imri is a man of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time of the return from the Babylonian exile. He is the father of Omri and the son of Bani, making him an ancestor of one of Nehemiah's helpers during the reconstruction of Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 9:4).
H0566G.origine: The name Imri means "eloquent" in Hebrew, evoking one who speaks well or with authority. He belongs to a family of the tribe of Judah that survived the exile and participated in the return and restoration of Israel.
H0566G.emploi: Imri appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 9:4, where he is presented as a link in the genealogy of the families that resettled in Jerusalem after the return from Babylon. His name is included in the lineage that contributed to the reconstruction of the temple and the Israelite community.

sens: man of Judah during the Exile and Return
H0566H.detail: Imri is a man of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when Nehemiah organizes the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem after the return from Exile. He is known as the father of Zaccur, who actively participated in this reconstruction work (Nehemiah 3:2). His name appears simply to identify the lineage of one of the workers engaged in this major restoration effort.
H0566H.origine: The name Imri means "eloquent" in Hebrew, derived from a root evoking speech and expression. It is a typical name from the post-exilic context, a period when the Jews returned from Babylonian captivity reorganized and rebuilt their community.
H0566H.emploi: Imri appears only once in the entire Bible, in Nehemiah 3:2, where he is mentioned as the father of Zaccur. In this context, he represents a family of Judah engaged in the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah's leadership, probably in the fifth century B.C. His brief but significant appearance marks his indirect participation in this major community restoration.

sens: People of Canaan established east of the Jordan and in the mountainous regions
Inhabitants of the lands that God promised to Israel
Military adversaries that the Israelites faced during the conquest
H0567.detail:
1. The Amorites are a Canaanite people mentioned as early as Genesis 10:16, one of the peoples who occupied Canaan before the arrival of the Israelites. They primarily inhabited the lands east of the Jordan and the mountainous regions, forming kingdoms ruled by powerful kings like Sihon (Numbers 21:21).

2. God promises Abraham that these lands will be given to his descendants (Genesis 15:16), but on the condition that "the iniquity of the Amorites has come to its full measure." This is why the Lord entrusts Israel with the mission to drive them out.

3. During the conquest of Canaan, the Amorites appear as the main military obstacles to the Israelites. Joshua describes them as formidable adversaries, and the Bible recounts how God intervenes to defeat them: "I sent the hornets ahead of you, which drove them out before you" (Joshua 24:12). After the conquest, some Amorites remain and live in peace with Israel (1 Samuel 7:14).
H0567.origine: The name "Amorites" comes from the root "Amor" and literally means "inhabitants of the heights" or "say-ers" (those who say). This people bore a name related to geography (the mountainous regions of Canaan) or to speech. The Amorites are among the ten peoples listed in Genesis 10 as descendants of Canaan, alongside the Jebusites, Girgashites, and others.
H0567.emploi: The word "Amorites" appears about 90 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the books of the Pentateuch (Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy) and in the history of the conquest (Joshua and Judges). It refers both to an entire people and to the specific kingdoms of Sihon and Og. In Exodus 3:8 and 13:5, God announces to Israel that He will deliver them from the Amorites. In Judges and 1 Samuel, the Amorites persist as a neighboring people to Israel, often in conflict or in peace depending on the circumstances. The name also symbolizes the obstacle that God helps Israel to overcome.
H0567.portee: The Amorites remind the reader that God keeps His promises by giving Israel the land of Canaan, but also that He judges peoples for their sins (Genesis 15:16). Their history illustrates God's faithfulness and the military power of the Lord who fights for His people. It also shows that faith in God prevails over the apparent strength of adversaries: Israel does not conquer Canaan by its own valor, but by divine intervention.

sens: Man of the tribe of Levi during the united monarchy
Ancestor of Zadok in the priestly genealogy
H0568G.detail:
1. Amaria is a man of the tribe of Levi who lived during the united monarchy in Israel. He is mentioned in the genealogy of the priests of Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 6:7 and 6:52) as the son of Meraioth and the father of Ahitub.
2. He is the ancestor of Zadok, the high priest under King David. His place in this priestly genealogy shows that he belongs to an important family of priests in the temple worship.
H0568G.origine: The name Amaria means "Jehovah speaks" or "Yah has promised," composed of the divine name Yah (short form of Jehovah) and a verb meaning "to say" or "to speak." It is a typical theophoric name among the Hebrews, placing the divine name within the person's name to express a blessing or an act of God.
H0568G.emploi: Amaria appears twice in the Bible, both times in 1 Chronicles 6, in the genealogy of the Levitical priests. These two verses provide the same genealogical information: he is the son of Meraioth and the father of Ahitub. This position in the priestly succession was important, as it established the legitimacy of the priests of the temple of Jerusalem in the lineage of Levi.

sens: Man of the tribe of Levi living during the divided monarchy
Name meaning "God speaks" or "Yah has promised"
H0568H.detail:
1. Amaria is a man belonging to the tribe of Levi, whose several descendants played important roles in the Israelite priesthood. He is an ancestor in a long priestly lineage: in 1 Chronicles 6:11, he is presented as the son of Azariah and the father of Ahitub, part of the genealogy of the temple priests.
2. His Hebrew name literally means "God speaks" or "Yah has promised" — it is an affirmation that the Lord has committed Himself by His word. This name reflects the faith of the parents who named him, expressing their trust in the divine promise.
H0568H.origine: The name Amaria is composed of two Hebrew elements: "amar" (to say, to speak) and "Yah" (short form of the name of God, Yahweh). This construction is typical of Hebrew theophoric names, where the name of God is associated with a divine action. The name thus expresses the idea that God speaks or commits Himself by His promise to the bearer or his family.
H0568H.emploi: Amaria primarily appears in the priestly genealogies of the Old Testament. In 1 Chronicles 6:11, he is mentioned as a link in a genealogical chain of priests. In Ezra 7:3, he reappears in the lineage of the priest Ezra, confirming his importance in the priestly line. These occurrences place him in the context of the divided monarchy and beyond, in a time when the priestly ministry was central to the religious life of Israel.
H0568H.portee: The name of Amaria reminds us that God speaks and keeps His promises. For the Christian reader, it is an invitation to remember that the word of God has already been fulfilled in the history of Israel and its priestly lineage, announcing the priesthood of Christ described in the New Testament.

sens: Levite, son of Hebron
Member of the tribe of Levi at the time of the Exodus and in the wilderness
H0568I.detail:
1. Amaria is a Levite, meaning a member of the tribe of Levi, who lived during the time of the Exodus and in the wilderness. His father was named Hebron, and he had three brothers: Jeriah, Jahaziel, and Jekameam (1 Chronicles 23:19).
2. In the genealogy of the priestly families, Amaria is mentioned as the second son of Hebron, after Jeriah who was the chief (1 Chronicles 24:23). He represents one of the important branches of the Levitical descent.
H0568I.origine: The name Amaria means "Yah has promised" or "Jehovah speaks": it combines "Amar" (to say, to promise) and "Yah" (the name of God). This name expresses trust in God's word and promises. Several important figures in Israel bore this name, including a high priest under Jehoshaphat and the father of Zephaniah.
H0568I.emploi: Amaria is a name borne by several descendants of Levi. This one, son of Hebron, is mentioned only in the genealogies of Chronicles (1 Chronicles 23:19 and 24:23) as one of the four sons of Hebron who played a role in organizing the service of the Levites at the temple. His name appears in the lists of those responsible for the order of worship and the administration of the sanctuary.
H0568I.portee: This name reminds us that God's promise and His word are at the heart of the life of the chosen people. The Levites who bore this name embodied sacred service and reminded Israel that God has spoken and kept His promises to His people.

sens: High priest during the reign of King Jehoshaphat
H0568J.detail: Amaria is a high-ranking chief priest mentioned during the reign of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. He is designated as "the chief priest" (2 Chronicles 19:11), meaning he is the highest authority in the worship and religious affairs of the kingdom. Alongside Zebadiah, who oversees the king's civil affairs, Amaria supervises everything concerning the Lord and the observance of the Law.
H0568J.origine: The Hebrew name Amaria (אֲמַרְיָהוּ) literally means "the Lord speaks" or "Yah has promised," composed of two elements: "amar" (word, promise) and "Yah" (short form of the divine name). It is a theophoric name, very common in Israel, celebrating the action or word of God.
H0568J.emploi: Amaria appears only once in the Scriptures, in 2 Chronicles 19:11. The context shows that King Jehoshaphat appointed him as chief priest to exercise religious authority and judge matters concerning the worship of the Lord. He represents the theocratic structure of Judah, where spiritual power and temporal power are distinct but complementary: the priest oversees God's Law, while the civil leader manages the affairs of the kingdom.

sens: Man who lived during the divided monarchy in Israel
H0568K.detail: Amaria is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 31:15. He is a man of responsibility, placed in charge of distributions in the priestly cities under the reign of King Hezekiah. His role was to ensure, along with other officials, that the portions of food and shares due to the priests and Levites were faithfully distributed to all their brethren, young and old, according to their respective divisions.
H0568K.origine: The name Amaria (אֲמַרְיָהוּ) literally means "Yah has spoken" or "Yah has promised," composed of the Hebrew verb "to speak, to say" and the divine Yah (abbreviated from the divine name). It is a theophoric name characteristic of the biblical era, expressing a promise or divine word addressed to the parents of the newborn.
H0568K.emploi: Amaria appears only in 2 Chronicles 31:15, in the context of the religious reforms of King Hezekiah. He is listed among officials responsible for distributing to the priests and Levites their shares in the priestly cities. His mention in this administrative list indicates that he held an important position in the organization of worship and the maintenance of the clergy under this reforming king.

sens: Man who lived during the time of the Exile and Return
H0568L.detail: Amaria is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:42, among those who had taken foreign wives and had to repudiate them after the return from Exile. His name appears alongside Shallum and Joseph in this list of repentance.
H0568L.origine: The name Amaria means "Yah has promised" or "Yahweh speaks," composed of two elements: "Amar" (to say, to speak) and "Yah" (abbreviation of the divine name Yahweh). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing trust in God's word and promise.
H0568L.emploi: Amaria appears only once in the biblical texts that have come down to us, in Ezra 10:42. He is listed among the Israelites who, after the return from exile in Babylon, had married foreign women and agreed to repudiate them to obey the Law. This passage shows a moment of spiritual crisis and religious reform under the leadership of Ezra.

sens: Priest who sealed the covenant under Nehemiah
Head of a priestly family at the return from Exile
H0568M.detail:
1. Amaria is a Jewish priest mentioned three times in the book of Nehemiah, during the time of the return from Exile to Jerusalem (5th century B.C.). He is among those who signed or sealed the covenant made after the restoration of the Temple (Nehemiah 10:3), alongside other religious leaders like Pashhur and Malchijah.
2. He is also listed as the head of a priestly family: in Nehemiah 12:2, he is named among the high priests who returned with Zerubbabel, and in Nehemiah 12:13, we see that his family bore the name Johanan in the next generation. This shows the importance of his position in the hierarchy of the restored Temple.
H0568M.origine: The name Amaria means "Yahweh speaks" or "Yah has promised" in Hebrew: it is composed of Amar ("to say, to speak") and Yah (the abbreviated divine name). It is a typical theophoric name of the time, expressing trust in God's word and promises. Several men bore this name in Israel's history, but this one is particularly marked by the context of the return from Exile.
H0568M.emploi: Amaria is mentioned exclusively in the book of Nehemiah, in chapter 10 (v. 3), 12 (v. 2 and 13). He always appears in official lists or records: first among the signers of the solemn covenant after the reconstruction of the Temple, then in the genealogy of the priests who returned with Zerubbabel at the end of the Babylonian Exile. These three occurrences clearly situate him in the administrative and religious context of the return and restoration of Jerusalem in the 5th century B.C., where priestly genealogies held great importance for the order of worship.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah at the time of the exile and return
H0568N.detail: Amaria is a man of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, during the return from exile to Jerusalem. He is the son of Shephatiah and the father of Zechariah, and belongs to the lineage of the descendants of Perez who resettled in the holy city after the Babylonian captivity (Nehemiah 11:4).
H0568N.origine: The name Amaria means "Yahweh speaks" or "Yah has promised," composed of two Hebrew elements: Amar (to speak) and Yah (abbreviation of the divine name Yahweh). This same name was borne by several important men in Israel's history: a high priest under Jehoshaphat, another under Hezekiah, and other religious figures, which shows that it was an honorable name in priestly and Judean families.
H0568N.emploi: Amaria is mentioned only once in the provided usages: in Nehemiah 11:4, where he appears in the genealogy of Athajah, one of the sons of Judah who settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile. This passage lists the families who reclaimed the city, and Amaria represents a link in the genealogical chain connecting the former inhabitants to the restored community of God's people.

sens: Ancestor of Zephaniah, mentioned in the genealogy of the prophet
H0568O.detail: Amaria is a character from the Old Testament known only by his mention in the genealogy of Zephaniah. He is the son of Hezekiah and the grandfather of Gedaliah, according to the lineage reported in Zephaniah 1:1. His name appears in the genealogical chain that establishes the lineage of the prophet Zephaniah, without the Bible reporting any other details about his life or role.
H0568O.origine: The name Amaria literally means "Yah has spoken" or "Yah has promised," combining the Hebrew verb "amar" (to say, to speak) and the divine name "Yah." It is a common theophoric name in Israelite tradition, expressing the idea that God has spoken or committed to this person or their family.
H0568O.emploi: Amaria is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Zephaniah 1:1, where he appears in the genealogy of the prophet Zephaniah. He is identified as the son of Hezekiah and appears four generations before the prophet. This unique mention shows that the author of Zephaniah wishes to establish the genealogical legitimacy of the prophet by tracing his descent back to a notable figure, likely King Hezekiah.

sens: King of Shinar (Babylonia) at the time of the Patriarchs
H0569.detail: Amraphel is the king of Shinar, an ancient region of Babylonia, mentioned during the time of Abraham. He is one of the four kings who conspire to fight Kedorlaomer and the kings of the region (Genesis 14:1 and 14:9). His name literally means "the one who speaks of darkness" or "the one who pronounces the fall," according to ancient etymological traditions. Historians often assume he is the king Hammurabi of Babylon (circa 2100 B.C.), although this identification remains debated.
H0569.origine: The name Amraphel comes from Hebrew and traditionally means "the one who speaks of darkness" or "fall of the sayer" — an imaginative composition that could evoke either a power of speech related to darkness or a declaration of ruin. Some traditions link it to Akkadian names or ancient royal titles, reflecting contacts between Near Eastern cultures. The name remains enigmatic: no familial link is established in the biblical text.
H0569.emploi: Amraphel appears only twice in the Bible, both times in the account of Genesis 14, which recounts the war between the kings of Mesopotamia. In Genesis 14:1, he is presented as king of Shinar at the time when four kings rise against five others. In Genesis 14:9, he appears again among the four allied kings who confront Kedorlaomer. The context is political and military: Amraphel represents one of the great powers of the time, contemporary with Abraham. His role is purely narrative — he illustrates the historical context in which the Patriarchs move.
H0569.portee: Amraphel reminds the reader that the Patriarchs lived in a world of real political powers, with their wars and alliances. His mention anchors the story of Abraham in the ancient history of the Near East and shows that no human force, even that of great kings, is outside of God's will to protect His people.

sens: The day that preceded the present day
The night that has just passed
A recent or close past, in a figurative sense
H0570.detail:
1. The primary meaning is the day immediately before today. When Laban says to Jacob, "Yesterday, the God of your father spoke to me" (Genesis 31:29), he is referring to the previous day, the moment just passed when God addressed him. It is a concrete and precise temporal marker.
2. The word also refers to the night that has just elapsed: "I lay with my father last night," says the eldest daughter of Lot (Genesis 19:34). Here, "yesterday" applies to the night, to that dark period of the old day that has ended.
3. In a figurative sense, the word evokes a past that is receding, a long-gone era. In Job 30:3, it speaks of places "long abandoned," as if the abandonment dates back to "yesterday" in a broad sense: to an ancient and now distant time. It is the idea of time slipping away and what belongs to the past.
H0570.origine: The Hebrew word אֶמֶשׁ comes from a root expressing the idea of the day or evening that is passing. It designates the day that has gone by, one that has slipped behind us. The formation of the word suggests the movement of time: what was in front of oneself becomes behind oneself.
H0570.emploi: The word appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the narratives of the Book of Genesis and in face-to-face speech (Genesis 19:34; 31:29 and 31:42). Laban uses it twice to refer to the immediate proximity of a divine event, reinforcing the immediacy of the memory. Jehu also uses it to recall an ancient crime: "I saw yesterday the blood of Naboth" (2 Kings 9:26), as if the murder, although past, remained present in his memory. In Job 30:3, the meaning broadens towards a more vague duration, an indefinite but bygone past.
H0570.portee: This humble yet evocative word reminds us how quickly time passes and how brief our days are. "Yesterday" can refer to what has just passed, but it also speaks of what will never return. For the believer, this invites us not to forget what God has done "yesterday," to remain attentive to the acts of His providence, and not to take the present for granted.

sens: Quality of one who keeps promises and remains loyal
Solidarity and stability, what endures
Truth, agreement between words and reality
Reliability, trustworthy character
Sincerity, integrity in conduct
H0571G.detail:
1. Faithfulness is the quality of one who keeps their word and remains loyal to someone. It is the commitment that persists. Abraham's servant prays to God saying: "who has not withdrawn his mercy and faithfulness toward my lord" (Genesis 24:27), showing that God's faithfulness guarantees the fulfillment of His promises.
2. It is also solidity and permanence, what remains firm. The commandments of the Lord are "Established forever, Made with faithfulness and uprightness" (Psalms 111:8), showing that faithfulness is inseparable from stability.
3. Faithfulness can mean truth, the exact agreement between what is said and what is real. In Jeremiah 10:10, "the Lord is the God of truth" emphasizes that God is absolutely reliable in every word.
4. It also expresses reliability, that which can be counted on without fear. A king "judges faithfully the poor" (Proverbs 29:14): he fulfills his duty without failing.
5. Finally, it is integrity in conduct and relationships with others. Nehemiah remembers: "You have been just in all that has come upon us, for you have shown faithfulness" (Nehemiah 9:33), confessing the justice and sincerity of divine governance.
H0571G.origine: The Hebrew word אֱמֶת comes from the root אמן (āman), which means "to be firm, to be stable." This root evokes the image of what holds firm, what does not collapse. From the same root come "amen" (affirmation of what is true and stable) and "emet" in the feminine. The fundamental concept is that of stability — moral, factual, relational — which inspires trust and certainty.
H0571G.emploi: This word appears 66 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms, Proverbs, and historical books. It primarily denotes God's faithfulness to His commitments: it accompanies His mercy (Exodus 34:6, Psalms 86:15) and supports His throne (Psalms 61:8). Then, the Bible praises the faithfulness of men toward God or others: Nehemiah was found "faithful" (Nehemiah 7:2), and a king must judge "faithfully" (Proverbs 29:14). The word also shifts towards the meaning of "truth" in a doctrinal sense: the ordinances of the Lord are made "with faithfulness and uprightness" (Psalms 111:8). Finally, it can mean "sincerity" in the service rendered (2 Chronicles 31:20) or in testimonies (Isaiah 38:3). In all these cases, the core remains the same: a reliable conformity between promise and fact, between heart and action.
H0571G.portee: Faithfulness is at the heart of the relationship with God. This word reminds the believer that divine promises are not empty words: they are anchored in the very nature of God, solid and permanent. It also invites the believer to cultivate the same faithfulness in their own life — toward God, toward their brothers, toward their responsibilities — by imitating the unwavering loyalty of the Lord. It is a word that transforms abstract trust into practical security: one can rely on the true God.

sens: Certainty and reliability of what is affirmed or promised
Conformity of the word to the reality of facts
Faithfulness and constancy in commitment
Moral uprightness and integrity in actions
Authentic knowledge of God and His ways
Word or doctrine in accordance with divine will
H0571H.detail: 1. Truth as certainty: it is what is sure, reliable, and does not deceive. When Abraham asks God to lead him "faithfully" to the right bride (Genesis 24:48), he trusts in the reality of the divine promise. 2. Truth as conformity to facts: it is the word that states things as they really are. When the queen says to King Solomon, "It was indeed true what I heard" (2 Chronicles 9:5), she acknowledges that what she had heard corresponded exactly to reality. 3. Truth as faithfulness: it is keeping one's word, remaining constant in commitments. It is the foundation of trust between people. 4. Moral truth: it is acting with uprightness and justice, without lies or deception. Zechariah asks the Judeans to "speak the truth to one another" and to "render true judgments in your gates" (Zechariah 8:16 and 8:19). 5. Spiritual truth: it is authentically knowing God and His ways. Psalm 51:8 expresses this desire: "You desire truth in the inward parts." 6. Truth as doctrine: it is the true teaching of God, which guides toward wisdom and justice (Proverbs 22:21).
H0571H.origine: The Hebrew word אמֶת comes from a root expressing the idea of solidity and stability. Its primary image is that of something solid, stable, that does not collapse. Hence its meaning of faithfulness: one who is reliable is like a stable foundation. In biblical Hebrew, this word is closely related to the idea of trust and security: a true word is a word upon which one can build. The family of the word includes terms denoting certainty and fulfillment.
H0571H.emploi: The word אמֶת appears 48 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms, Proverbs, and prophetic books. It is used to describe the word of God that fulfills His promises (Genesis 24:48), the necessity of truthful testimony in justice (Deuteronomy 17:4; Proverbs 14:25), and the importance of speaking the truth among humans (Zechariah 8:16). In the Psalms and Proverbs, truth is presented as a good that one seeks, loves, and learns. Among the prophets, especially Jeremiah and Isaiah, God's truth contrasts with the lies of idols and false prophets: there is no one who "calls for justice" or "pleads for truth" (Isaiah 59:4).
H0571H.portee: For the Christian, this word reveals that truth is not a philosophical abstraction, but the very characteristic of God Himself and the foundation of trust. To speak truth, to live truth, to seek God's truth in one's heart is to participate in what is at the core of divine nature. The Bible invites everyone to honor truth in their words and actions, for it is thus that justice and peace are built in human communities.

sens: What is firm, stable, durable, on which one can rely
What is faithful, loyal, trustworthy
What is true, in accordance with reality
The true word, the right teaching
The ordinances and laws of God
The peace and security that result from it
H0571I.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes what is firm and holds strong, like a solid foundation: what remains, what is stable and permanent. It conveys the idea of solidity and permanence. In Isaiah 39:8, when the king says, "the word of the Lord is good," he acknowledges that this word rests on something secure and lasting.
2. Truth is also what can be considered certain because the one who speaks it is faithful and loyal. It embodies the idea of reliability: one can count on this word, it will not deceive. This describes the nature of God who always keeps His promises.
3. Truth corresponds to reality, what is true as opposed to falsehood or error. In the Psalms, "the judgments of the Lord are true" (19:10) means that they are just and in accordance with the reality of what is good.
4. It is the true word, which states things as they are and does not deceive anyone. The "just ordinances and laws of truth" given at Sinai (Nehemiah 9:13) are true commandments, that is, just and righteous.
5. The word also denotes true teaching, faithful doctrine, authentic religious knowledge. "Your law is truth" (Psalms 119:151) means that all of God's teaching is true, complete, and trustworthy.
6. From this truth of God and His word flows peace and security: the one who relies on God's firm promise can live in certainty and rest (2 Kings 20:19).
H0571I.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes solidity and stability, the idea of something that holds firm and does not collapse. The same word family gives the adjective "true" and the noun "faith" (that on which one relies). The Hebrew word expresses both objective reality (what is true) and reliable trust (that on which one can count): for the ancient Hebrew, these two ideas are inseparable. What is true is what endures; what is faithful is what can be believed.
H0571I.emploi: The word appears about 11 times in the Segond. It is mainly used in the Psalms and historical books to speak of God's word and commandments. In 2 Samuel 7:28, the king acknowledges that "Your words are truth" — affirming that God speaks what is, that His promise holds. In the Psalms, "truth" qualifies judgments (19:10), righteousness (119:142), and God's commandments (119:151), emphasizing their solidity and absolute reliability. In Nehemiah 9:13, the "laws of truth" are the commandments that God gave at Sinai, presented as just and truly saving. The word is also used for the divine promise that calms and reassures (2 Kings 20:19). Everywhere, it describes what remains firm and faithful.
H0571I.portee: This word teaches us that truth is not merely a matter of intellectual accuracy: it is primarily solidity, reliability, loyalty. When the Bible says that God and His word are truth, it assures us that we can count on Him, that His promises hold, that His teaching will not deceive us. It is an invitation to trust and peace: to lean on the truth of God is to lean on an unshakeable rock.

sens: Soft, closed container for transporting goods, especially grains
Container that can be filled, closed, and carried with one on a journey
H0572.detail:
1. The word denotes a sack, that is, a container made of fabric or soft material used to transport and store things — here, grains and money. Joseph's brothers each bring down their sack (Genesis 44:11) and open them: these are objects that are handled, loaded and unloaded, inspected. Money can slip into the opening of the sack, at the discretion of men or the Lord (Genesis 43:23: "Your God, the God of your father, who has given you a treasure in your sacks").
2. The sack also refers to the contents of this container: when speaking of "the money of the sack" or "the money of each according to his weight" found "at the entrance of the sack" (Genesis 43:21), it designates both the sack itself and what it contains. It is a humble but essential object of ancient travel and commerce.
H0572.origine: The Hebrew word אַמְתַּחַת (amtahat) comes from a root meaning to stretch or spread out — the initial image is that of something being spread or filled. In Hebrew, this word appears mainly in the account of Joseph in Egypt: it is a concrete term from the everyday vocabulary of the ancient Near East, designating a practical and familiar object.
H0572.emploi: The word appears twelve times in the Bible, exclusively in the account of Genesis 42-44, where Joseph's brothers go to Egypt to buy grain. Joseph, now governor, orders that the sacks be filled with grain and that their money be secretly placed in them — a riddle that first terrifies the brothers, convinced they have stolen or are bringing misfortune. The word "sack" recurs constantly: they open the sacks (Genesis 42:27 and 44:11), they bring them down, they find the money. It is the silent sign of Joseph's hidden wisdom and kindness towards his family.
H0572.portee: This humble word reminds us that God often acts through the concrete and material details of life: a sack, a piece of money, a journey. The reappearance of money in the brothers' sacks becomes a sign of divine providence, which provides for our needs without our initially understanding it. It is a lesson against fear and unbelief: what seems like a disaster can be a gift from the Lord.

sens: father of the prophet Jonah
H0573.detail: Amitthai is the father of the prophet Jonah. He appears twice in the Bible: first in 2 Kings 14:25, where he is presented as the father of Jonah, the prophet who announced to King Jeroboam II the restoration of Israel's borders; then at the beginning of the book of Jonah (Jonah 1:1), where the word of the Lord is addressed to Jonah, son of Amitthai. Although not well known in himself, Amitthai is remembered in the Bible solely as the father of this unique prophet sent to Nineveh.
H0573.origine: The name Amitthai means "my truth" in Hebrew: it comes from the root "emet" (אֱמֶת), which expresses truth, reliability, and certainty. It is a name that carries within it the values of divine faithfulness and certainty, particularly fitting for the father of a prophet called to proclaim the word of the Lord.
H0573.emploi: Amitthai is mentioned exactly twice in the Bible. In 2 Kings 14:25, he is identified as the father of the prophet Jonah, in the context of the reign of Jeroboam II, king of Israel. In Jonah 1:1, the same familial link introduces the account of the prophet Jonah. No personal details about Amitthai himself are provided: the Bible knows him only through his connection to the famous prophet he fathered.

sens: That inspires intense terror, a deep fear
That causes dread by its brute force or destructive power
That provokes horror by its threatening or overwhelming nature
H0574.detail:
1. The word describes what inspires intense terror, a fear that seizes the one who sees it: it is the feeling of fright in the presence of something extraordinary and threatening. In Daniel 7:7, the fourth beast is described as "terrifying" because its mere appearance provokes fear and dread.
2. It is also what causes dread through its brute force and destructive power. The beast terrifies not only by its appearance but by what it does: it devours, crushes, tramples. Its destructive nature makes it monstrous and formidable.
3. The word finally evokes the horror provoked by an overwhelming, inhuman, insurmountable character. This beast is "different from all the previous animals," endowed with a power that exceeds the ordinary: it is this threatening otherness that makes it "terrifying."
H0574.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses intense fear and terror. It belongs to the family of words that describe religious dread, deep fear in the face of what is extraordinary or supernatural. It is a rare adjective that carries the full weight of the feeling of horror and fright.
H0574.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Daniel 7:7. It qualifies the fourth beast of Daniel's vision, which represents a future empire (generally identified as the Roman Empire in traditional Christian interpretation). The uniqueness of this usage underscores the exceptional nature of this beast: it is so extraordinary, so formidable in its destructive power, that it can only be described by this rare and intensive word. The apocalyptic context of Daniel amplifies the significance of the term: it is an unparalleled, monstrous, and terrifying beast.
H0574.portee: This word reminds the reader that human power, even the most formidable and overwhelming in the eyes of the world, remains a visible and material creature that a true believer should not fear more than God. Daniel's vision teaches that earthly empires, as terrifying as they may be, are beasts that pass away, while the Kingdom of God remains eternal. The word "terrifying" invites the reader not to be paralyzed by the apparent power of evil or oppression, but to place their trust in the One who judges.

sens: At what place, what location?
To what place, in what direction?
Until what time, how long?
On which side, which one?
H0575.detail:
1. At what place, what location? — The word poses the question of location: where is someone or something. For example, Gehazi asks Elisha "where have you come from" (2 Kings 5:25), seeking to know where he has returned from.

2. To what place, in what direction? — The question concerns movement: where someone is going, in what direction they are headed. The angel asks Hagar "where are you going" (Genesis 16:8), and the brothers ask "where has your beloved gone" (Song of Solomon 6:1).

3. Until what time, how long? — The word applies to time: until when will a situation last. Job cries out "how long will you afflict my soul" (Job 19:2), expressing his impatience in the face of suffering.

4. On which side, which one? — Applied to space in a more vague manner, the word asks which side something is located on. When Gehazi says he went "neither one side nor the other" (2 Kings 5:25), he designates the directions without precision.
H0575.origine: The Hebrew word אָן (an) is a primitive interrogative particle, related to the idea of asking for direction or a moment. Its etymology traces back to a root expressing movement or the search for location. This type of interrogative particle appears in many Semitic languages and serves as a basis for asking open questions about place or time. Its family includes forms related to general inquiry.
H0575.emploi: This word appears 33 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in dialogues and narrative accounts. It is first used to ask for a specific place (Genesis 16:8, 1 Samuel 10:14), then for a direction (Deuteronomy 1:28, Song of Solomon 6:1). It also applies to the duration of time (Job 19:2, Psalms 13:2-3). The psalms use it in cries of helplessness or distress (Psalms 139:7: "where can I flee from your presence"). The temporal usage expresses impatience in the face of suffering or waiting (Habakkuk 1:2: "how long shall I cry out"). This word marks an open question, without a presupposed answer.
H0575.portee: This simple particle highlights the human condition: we seek our way, we ask when suffering will end, we do not know where to go. It expresses the anxious expectation of the believer before God and the urgency of their questions. The psalmist who asks "where can I flee from your presence" (Psalms 139:7) acknowledges that God is everywhere. These honest questions of the heart find their answer in God alone.

sens: first-person singular personal pronoun
emphasis on the subject or the speaker
solemn or emphatic affirmation
H0576B.detail:
1. The word is simply the pronoun "me" or "I" in Aramaic, used to designate the speaker. It is found in place of the verb that already indicates the person: "I, Darius, have issued this decree" (Ezra 6:12) rather than simply "I have issued."
2. Placed before or after the verb, this pronoun can reinforce the subject to bring it to the forefront: "I, Nebuchadnezzar, was at ease" (Daniel 4:4) emphasizes that it is indeed the king himself, with all his weight and pride, who speaks.
3. Often used to give solemnity to a statement, as when a king affirms a decree or a truth: "If this secret has been revealed to me" (Daniel 2:30) or "Is this not Babylon the great, which I have built?" (Daniel 4:30), the pronoun underscores the importance of what is being said.
H0576B.origine: It is the Aramaic equivalent of the Hebrew pronouns אָנִי (ani) and אָנֹכִי (anokhi) which both mean "I" or "me." The word belongs to the group of personal pronouns, fundamental forms of language. In Aramaic, spoken in Babylon during the exile, this pronoun takes the form אֲנָה (anah) and is used, as in Hebrew, to emphasize the identity of the speaker.
H0576B.emploi: This word appears 16 times in the Bible, exclusively in passages in Aramaic: the book of Ezra (verses of royal decrees) and the book of Daniel (speeches and narratives). It is mainly found in the solemn declarations of kings (Darius, Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon) or in the reported speech of Daniel himself. The emphasis is constant: these characters use it to give weight to their words, to remind of their authority, or to underscore what they affirm. Sometimes it is rendered in English as "I" or "I've," sometimes as "me" depending on the context and the placement of the pronoun.
H0576B.portee: This small word reminds us that in Scripture, even great kings (Nebuchadnezzar, Darius) express themselves through this pronoun. This shows the importance of the first person and personal responsibility in the declaration: one cannot hide behind the impersonal. For the modern reader, it is a reminder that every engaging word — whether from a king or from the prophet Daniel — carries the personal implication of the one who pronounces it.

sens: A call addressed to someone to attract their attention
A pleading imploration addressed to God
An exclamation expressing a strong emotion or a pressing wish
H0577.detail:
1. This word is an interjection, which is a kind of cry uttered in speech to call someone or to express a feeling. It marks the beginning of a respectful or affectionate address: "O Lord!" (2 Kings 20:3), "O Lord, do not let us perish" (Jonah 1:14). It is as if one is saying, "Listen to me!" or "Look toward me!"
2. When a believer prays to God, they often begin their prayer with this interjection to show that they are addressing Him with respect and urgency. Hezekiah says: "O Lord! Remember that I have walked before You in faithfulness" (Isaiah 38:3), seeking to awaken the Lord's attention to his serious situation. It is a cry from the heart that says: "I turn to You!"
3. Sometimes it expresses an intense feeling or a fervent desire: it can serve to implore, to plead, to protest, or to call out with passion.
H0577.origine: This interjection is ancient in Hebrew. It belongs to the language of prayer and respectful address. Its use has been preserved in liturgy and biblical prayer as a means of expressing reverence and urgency when addressing God or a superior. It creates a formal and pious distance between the speaker and the one to whom they are addressing.
H0577.emploi: The word appears twelve times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always in contexts of prayer or supplication. It is found among kings who implore God (Hezekiah in 2 Kings 20:3 and Isaiah 38:3), among prophets and priests (Nehemiah 1:11), and even among ordinary people in distress (the sailors in Jonah 1:14). It often opens a formal prayer, marking that the speaker is addressing God with seriousness and respect. Sometimes it also carries a nuance of reproach or passionate calling: Joseph hears a call for grace (Genesis 50:17).
H0577.portee: For a biblical reader, this word reminds us that authentic prayer begins with a sincere invocation: one does not address God in the usual tone of conversation, but with reverence and urgency. It is a call from the heart that acknowledges dependence on God. Seeing this word in a biblical prayer invites us to ask ourselves if we also pray with this respectful simplicity, recognizing to whom we are speaking and how much we need His listening ear.

sens: To emit plaintive sounds, groans
To express pain, sorrow through the voice
To manifest deep affliction, especially in mourning
H0578.detail:
1. The verb first describes the sound itself: low and continuous sounds that express suffering. It is the physical groaning, the audible complaint. At the gates of Zion, during divine judgment, the city itself seems to groan like a living creature (Isaiah 3:26).
2. More broadly, to groan is to externalize one's pain through the voice — to cry out inwardly one's sorrow. The fishermen "groan" when their means of livelihood collapses, when judgment strikes the Nile and dries up their income (Isaiah 19:8).
3. In both cases, it is the expression of an affliction that rises from the heart: the mourning of a ruined city, the lamentation of men deprived of resources. Groaning is the outward sign of inner desolation.
H0578.origine: The Hebrew root ānāh expresses the idea of audible complaint, lamentation. It is close to other ancient Hebrew words that denote suffering expressed vocally. Groaning is the natural sound of grief: it is through the voice that the broken heart speaks.
H0578.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, in the book of Isaiah, in contexts of divine judgment. In Isaiah 3:26, Zion itself groans during its desolation. In Isaiah 19:8, it is the men who groan in the face of the punishment that strikes them — groaning is the natural reaction to calamity, the spontaneous expression of a crushed heart.
H0578.portee: Groaning reminds us that pain has a voice, and that the groans of the suffering people rise up to God. This word shows that the Bible does not hide lamentation: it names it, it listens to it. For the believer, it is a call not to stifle one's pain, and to know that God hears those who groan under the weight of judgment or misfortune.

sens: to meet or find oneself face to face with someone or something
to occur, to happen (for an event, a misfortune)
to seek to provoke an occasion for dispute or conflict
H0579.detail:
1. To meet someone or something means to find oneself face to face with them. It is the idea of two things or beings crossing paths or being sent toward each other. In Exodus 21:13, the text speaks of a death "falling" into the hands of someone, meaning a death that has met this man by chance or by the will of God.
2. To occur means "to happen" or "to come to pass," referring to an event or misfortune. Psalms 91:10 promises that "no misfortune will befall" the believer, meaning that no evil will come to meet them. Similarly, Proverbs 12:21 asserts that no misfortune befalls the righteous: difficulties do not strike them.
3. To seek occasion means intentionally provoking or creating a pretext for dispute. In 2 Kings 5:7, the king of Israel says that Naaman "seeks occasion for dispute" with him: he is intentionally provoking a quarrel by sending him a request that the king cannot satisfy.
H0579.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of "meeting" or "coming face to face." Its primary meaning is spatial: two realities that come closer or collide. From there comes the figurative meaning of "to arrive" or "to occur" for events. The root expresses the aspect of movement toward or convergence.
H0579.emploi: This verb appears four times in the Hebrew Bible. It first describes a meeting or an event that occurs (Exodus 21:13 for an accidental death, Psalms 91:10 and Proverbs 12:21 for misfortunes that happen or do not happen). It is then used more actively to express the intention to seek or provoke: in 2 Kings 5:7, it is about "seeking occasion" for dispute. In all cases, the word evokes something that comes to meet, either by chance, by divine providence, or by malicious intent.
H0579.portee: These verses remind the believer that all events, whether happy or unfortunate, are either under God's control or the effect of human free will. Psalms 91:10 and Proverbs 12:21 offer a promise of protection: the one who fears God is not exposed to the same evils as the wicked. Conversely, the image of "seeking occasion" for dispute invites vigilance against those who intentionally seek conflict.

sens: Aramaic demonstrative pronoun referring to people or things that are distant ('those', 'those people')
Third person plural masculine personal pronoun ('them')
H0581A.detail:
1. This word is primarily a demonstrative pronoun: it designates specific people or things, often somewhat distant in the text or in thought. In Ezra 5:4, 'the' names refers to the specific names just mentioned — it is those names that are sought to be known. In Daniel 2:44, 'those kingdoms' points to the kingdoms previously described, those that the God of heaven will destroy.
2. This word also functions as a simple plural personal pronoun: it replaces a group of men or women already named. In Daniel 6:24, 'them, their children and their wives' clearly enumerates the accusers of Daniel and their families — the word 'them' precisely designates them.
H0581A.origine: It is an Aramaic word, the language spoken by the Jews after the exile. It corresponds exactly to the Hebrew word הֵמָּה (hem.mah), which means 'they' or 'them'. Aramaic has many similarities with Hebrew, and this pronoun is an example: same meaning, same basic grammatical structure, but pronounced in the Aramaic manner.
H0581A.emploi: This pronoun appears three times in the Aramaic New Testament (the portions of Ezra and Daniel written in Aramaic, not Hebrew). It appears in Ezra 5:4, Daniel 2:44, and Daniel 6:24. In Ezra, it serves to identify specific names; in Daniel, it designates either kingdoms or condemned persons. In each case, it refers to a plural masculine group, either demonstratively ('these') or purely pronominally ('them'). The French translation 'le' is an adaptation that sometimes reflects the definite article of the context rather than the pronominal force of the Aramaic word.

sens: feminine plural personal pronoun referring to several women or several feminine things
H0581B.detail: 1. This pronoun replaces a feminine plural subject or object. In Daniel 7:17, it refers to the four great beasts that will rise from the earth: the Aramaic text uses this pronoun to show that these creatures, although described in the feminine in Aramaic, form a group of acting entities. The pronoun allows the reader to understand that Daniel is speaking of several beings or powers collectively.
H0581B.origine: It is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew pronoun הֵמָּה (hemah, 'they'), adapted to the feminine gender. Aramaic was the language spoken and written in Mesopotamia and gradually in the Promised Land during the Persian period; several passages in the Book of Daniel are written in Aramaic rather than Hebrew. This pronoun belongs to the same family as other Aramaic personal pronouns that structure the sentence.
H0581B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 7:17, a passage where the prophet receives the interpretation of his vision of the four beasts. The context is that of a divine explanation: the angel Gabriel helps Daniel understand that these four fearsome animals represent four kings or four kingdoms that will dominate the earth. The use of the feminine plural pronoun reflects Aramaic grammar, where 'beasts' (חֵיוָן, chewyan) is of the feminine gender.
H0581B.portee: This passage shows how Daniel receives a supernatural understanding of future events. The four beasts symbolize human powers that God subjects to His judgment and replaces with His eternal kingdom. For the Christian reader, it is an assurance that the history of humanity does not last forever: temporal empires give way to the reign of Christ.

sens: an individual human being, male or female
an adult man, as opposed to a woman or child
a husband or companion
people, the crowd, persons in a group
humanity, the human race as a whole
a mortal, subject to death and weaknesses
H0582.detail:
1. The word primarily designates an individual human being, regardless of age or function. In Genesis 13:8, Abraham says to Lot: 'Let there be no strife between you and me'; he is speaking of concrete people who are part of their respective families.

2. Often it refers to an adult man in the strict sense, different from a woman or child. Ruth 1:11 clearly shows this: Naomi asks, 'Do I still have sons in my womb that they may be your husbands?' — here the word designates the life companion of a woman.

3. By extension, a man can be a husband, one who lives with a woman and starts a family with her. This meaning is found in the passage from Ruth.

4. The word is also used in the plural or to refer to a multitude: 'a very large crowd of people' (Ezra 10:1). It can then simply mean 'people', 'the world'.

5. In poetry or elevated language, it speaks of all humanity, of what is common to all humans. Isaiah 45:14 mentions 'the tall Sabeans': it refers to an entire people.

6. The word often carries the idea that man is mortal and weak, distinct from the gods: it is a being who lives, suffers, and dies, vulnerable and dependent.
H0582.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that refers to the idea of fragility and mortality. This is why some biblical scholars relate it to the verb that means 'to be weak' or 'to be sick'. The Aramaic has an equivalent word, 'enash', which also means 'man'. This term is distinct from another Hebrew word, 'ish' (אִישׁ), which emphasizes masculinity or social status, while 'enosh' focuses on the human condition itself: our mortality, our fragility, what we all have in common.
H0582.emploi: This word is one of the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible, used 531 times. It appears as early as Genesis to speak of the men Abraham encounters or of his servants. It is found in all historical books, poems, and prophets. Its use varies according to the context: sometimes it is an individual man ('there was a man', Genesis 24:32), sometimes a group ('the men of the city', Genesis 19:4), sometimes all humanity. In prophetic passages, the word can take on a deeper charge, highlighting the smallness of man before God or his mortal condition. Numbers 14:37 speaks of the spies who bring back an evil report: they are ordinary men whom God judges for their unbelief.
H0582.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on what it means to be human in the eyes of God. In Hebrew, 'enosh' carries the implicit idea of fragility and dependence: we are but mortals. It is an invitation to humility before the Creator. At the same time, the fact that God cares for these weak creatures, that He calls them by name, that He makes a covenant with them, reveals the magnitude of His grace. The word also reminds us of our shared responsibility: we are all men, all vulnerable, all called to give an account before God.

sens: Grandson of Adam, son of Seth
Man living before the Flood
Ancestor of Noah and all men after the Flood
H0583.detail: Enosh is the son of Seth and the grandson of Adam. He is born in the generations that immediately precede the Flood. His name means "man" in Hebrew, and he embodies humanity in ancient days. It is during the time of Enosh that men begin to call upon the name of the Lord (Genesis 4:26), marking an important moment in the relationship between God and humanity. Enosh fathers Kenan at ninety years old (Genesis 5:9), and then lives a total of nine hundred five years before he dies (Genesis 5:11). Through his lineage, he is one of the essential links in the chain that connects Adam to Noah, and through Noah to all men after the Flood.
H0583.origine: The Hebrew name אֱנוֹשׁ (Enosh) literally means "man," expressing mortal and fragile humanity. This word comes from the same root as the Hebrew word for "man" in general, emphasizing that this character represents the humanity of his time. His name reminds us of the human condition: created in the image of God, yet also subject to death.
H0583.emploi: Enosh appears seven times in the Bible, all occurrences found in the genealogy of Adam. He is first mentioned in Genesis 4:26, then appears in the list of generations from Genesis 5:6 to 5:11, which enumerates his birth, his descendants, and his lifespan. He is also mentioned in 1 Chronicles 1:1, in a genealogical recap. These passages present him as a crucial link in the human continuity before the Flood: each verse recalls his age at the birth of his son and the length of his life, thus establishing the uninterrupted genealogical thread from Adam.
H0583.portee: Enosh reminds us that humanity, even antediluvian, was capable of calling upon the name of the Lord and knowing Him. His presence in the genealogy of Christ (Luke 3:38) shows that God has followed the thread of redeemed humanity through the ages, even before the Flood. His story invites the reader to see that each generation, each person, is part of a long history of salvation that traces back to Adam and extends to Christ.

sens: To express pain, sorrow, or grief through muffled sounds
To lament a situation, to sigh in regret or sorrow
To languish, to weaken (for a plant or thing)
H0584.detail:
1. To groan is to emit dull and plaintive sounds to express physical or moral suffering. This is what the children of Israel do in Egypt: they groan under the yoke of slavery, their groans rise to God who hears them (Exodus 2:23). It is a cry from a broken heart.
2. The word can also mean to sigh in distress or regret in the face of a catastrophe or abomination. In besieged Jerusalem, those who groan because of the city's abominations receive a mark from God to be spared (Ezekiel 9:4). It expresses moral affliction in the face of evil.
3. Finally, to groan can describe the withering or weakening of something: the withered vine, which loses its vigor and beauty (Isaiah 24:7). It is a visible weakening.
H0584.origine: The Hebrew verb אָנַח (anahh) evokes the image of a sound that comes out with difficulty, muffled. It is a verb fundamentally linked to the expression of grief and sorrow. The root carries the idea of a complaint that rises from a afflicted heart.
H0584.emploi: This verb appears 12 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the books of lamentation and prophecy. In Exodus 2:23, the Israelite slaves groan under the weight of slavery, and God responds to their groans. In Lamentations (1:4, 1:8, 1:11, 1:21), Jerusalem itself and its people groan in the ruin of destruction. Ezekiel uses this verb to refer to those who lament over the abominations and those who groan in anticipation of divine judgment (9:4; 21:11-12). The Bible thus shows that to groan is the spontaneous expression of those who suffer and that God hears this groaning as a call.
H0584.portee: Biblical groaning is not weakness, but testimony: it acknowledges that suffering exists, that it is real, and that it cries out to God. Groaning recognizes that evil is intolerable and that only God can intervene. This is why God marks those who groan over abominations: He honors those whose conscience is sensitive to sin. For the Christian, groaning reminds us that prayer often begins not with elegant words, but with the cry of the heart.

sens: sound made by the body when breathing deeply and slowly, especially due to pain or fatigue
groan, complaint that expresses physical or moral suffering
expression of inner pain, grief that cannot be contained
sign of the weight of life and the despair of the one who suffers
H0585.detail:
1. A sigh is primarily a physical phenomenon: a deep and audible breath, as when the body relieves itself by exhaling air with effort. Job says that his sighs are his food (Job 3:24), in other words, he sighs constantly, so much that his suffering consumes him.

2. It is also a groan, a complaint that rises from a burdened heart. The psalmist grows weary of groaning; his nights are drenched with tears as he groans under the weight of his pain (Psalms 6:7 and 102:6).

3. A sigh is also the most authentic expression of inner disarray: what cannot be hidden or contained. The Lord knows all our sighs; they are not hidden from Him (Psalms 38:10).

4. In the laments, the sigh is the silent cry of one whom affliction strangles: the psalmist's years are consumed in sighs, his strength wears away (Psalms 31:11). It is the symptom of a broken heart.
H0585.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to sigh" or "to breathe heavily." It denotes the sound and gesture that involuntarily express pain: one cannot control their sighs when suffering is too strong. It is a word from the realm of raw emotion, linked to the body's breathing.
H0585.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the Old Testament, almost always in the psalms and laments. Job uses it to describe his extreme suffering (Job 3:24; 23:2). The psalmists use it to express their physical and spiritual distress: the body that is wasting away, the tears that flow, the sleepless night (Psalms 6:7; 31:11; 38:10; 102:6). Isaiah also uses it to depict human affliction, but sometimes to announce its end (Isaiah 35:10; 51:11). The sigh is always the sign of real and deep suffering.
H0585.portee: The sigh in the Bible is never despised: it is the truest expression of human suffering before God. Knowing that God hears our sighs and does not ignore them is a comfort: He sees our inner pain, the one we cannot always put into words. The sigh reminds us that the suffering Christian is not alone with their grief — God listens to what the heart expresses in silence.

sens: personal pronoun: first person plural
the speaker and others with him
H0586.detail:
1. This word is the pronoun "we" in Aramaic, the language in which certain passages of Daniel and Ezra are written. It refers to the speaker and others with him, just like the French "nous." In Ezra 4:16, the adversaries of the temple say: "We make known to the king" to speak as a group. In Daniel 3:16, the three young men respond to the king: "We have no need to answer you" — a "we" of unity and collective courage.
2. This pronoun often marks solidarity: in Ezra 5:11, the temple servants say "We are the servants of the God of heaven" to affirm their common identity and shared purpose. In Daniel 3:17, "We serve" and "our God" create a union of conviction in the face of danger.
H0586.origine: This word comes from the Aramaic spoken in the ancient Near East. It is very close to the Hebrew word for "we" (אֲנַחְנוּ, a.nach.nu, H0587) from which it shares the same root and almost the same form. Aramaic is a Semitic language related to Hebrew, spoken by the Jews after the exile. This pronoun simply expresses the collective identity of the speaker.
H0586.emploi: This word appears 4 times in the Aramaic New Testament — twice in Ezra (chapters 4 and 5) and twice in Daniel (chapter 3). In Ezra 4:16, the enemies of the Jewish people use "we" to present themselves as a united block before the king. In Ezra 5:11, the Jews respond with the same "we" to affirm their own unity. In Daniel 3, Daniel's three companions use "we" to stand together before the king: they will not respond individually, but as a united group in the face of idolatry. The pronoun retains its basic meaning, but its impact changes depending on who pronounces it and in what conflict.
H0586.portee: This simple pronoun illustrates the strength of unity. When the three young men say "We have no need," then "We serve our God," their "we" is not just grammar: it is the expression of a brotherhood in faith and a shared determination to stand firm in the face of persecution. For the reader, it reminds us that faithfulness to God is often affirmed not alone, but with others, and that this communion strengthens courage.

sens: Personal pronoun of the first person plural, designating the group that speaks or acts
Marks the inclusion or exclusion of one or more people within a group
Expresses common identity or solidarity among group members
Emphasizes a shared sense of belonging or collective responsibility
Reinforces the affirmation or protest of a group in a situation
H0587.detail: 1. The primary meaning is simply the designation of the group that speaks: the one speaking plus at least one other person. In Genesis 13:8, Abram says to Lot "we are brothers," expressing their kinship and common place in the same family. 2. Hebrew allows us to distinguish who is included or excluded from the group. In Isaiah 36:11, the three officers ask Rabshakeh to speak in Aramaic "for we understand it," designating themselves and excluding the listening people. 3. The word often reinforces shared identity or solidarity. In 1 Chronicles 11:1, Israel says to David "we are your bones and your flesh," affirming the unity of the people under their leader. 4. Sometimes "we" expresses collective responsibility in the face of the consequences of an action. In Numbers 20:4, the people complain: "Why have you brought the assembly of the Lord into this wilderness, for us to die there?" sharing the responsibility for the situation. 5. The word can also reinforce a common protest or request. In 1 Samuel 8:20, the people ask for a king saying "we will have a king," collectively affirming their desire against the will of the prophet.
H0587.origine: The Hebrew word אֲנַחְנוּ (anachnou) is a personal pronoun that appears in the earliest biblical texts. It comes from the root that simply designates the first person plural, with no known older etymology. This pronoun opposes the singular אֲנִי (ani, "I") and the dual אֲנַחְנוּ in its variants. Hebrew used this pronoun especially when it wanted to emphasize the group or create a marked opposition; often it omitted it when the verb alone sufficed to express the subject.
H0587.emploi: This pronoun appears about 115 times in the provided Hebrew text, mainly in historical and prophetic books. It is found in the narratives of Genesis when the patriarchs speak together or address others (Genesis 13:8, 42:11, 43:8), in Exodus and Numbers during the wilderness period (Numbers 20:4), in the books of Judges and Samuel during negotiations or collective decisions, and in the accounts of Ezra and Nehemiah when Israel engages in a common action or reflection. The pronoun often creates dramatic tension: in Nehemiah 4:23, Nehemiah emphasizes "we did not change our clothes" to show the constant vigilance of the people during the rebuilding. In 2 Kings 7:9, the lepers who discovered the spoils of the Syrians declare "what we are doing is not good," marking a collective moral shift. The use of the pronoun accentuates shared responsibility or a decision made together.
H0587.portee: This simple pronoun invites the believer to reflect on their belonging to the people of God. When Israel says "we are your bones and your flesh" to David, it reminds us of the importance of the unity of the body of Christ and the collective responsibility of Christians. When the people confess their sins in the plural, they acknowledge that sin and repentance engage the whole group, not just isolated individuals. This pronoun also speaks to us of solidarity: what we decide together, we bear together.

sens: City in the territory of Issachar or Naphtali
H0588.detail: Anacharath is a city mentioned only once in the Bible, during the division of the lands among the tribes of Israel. It appears in the list of cities assigned to the tribe of Issachar (Joshua 19:19).
H0588.origine: The name literally means "the groaning of fear" in ancient Hebrew. Its etymology reveals an image of desolation or distress associated with the place, although the biblical context does not develop its symbolic meaning.
H0588.emploi: Anacharath appears only once in Scripture, in Joshua 19:19, among the cities listed during the drawing of lots that assigns the lands to the twelve tribes after the conquest of Canaan. This mention is purely geographical and administrative: it serves to delineate the territory of Issachar. No particular biblical event is reported there.

sens: Personal pronoun of the first person singular, subject or complement of a verb
Marker of emphasis or personal insistence, highlighting the speaker in contrast to another
Affirmation of the identity or presence of the speaker
H0589.detail:
1. This is the basic pronoun used to refer to the one speaking in biblical Hebrew. It can be the subject of an action ("I will do") or the complement ("for me"), or even an attribute ("it is me"). For example, in Genesis 6:17, God says, "I, I will bring the flood," where the pronoun affirms that it is He, and no one else, who will act.
2. Often, this pronoun is used to emphasize the identity of the speaker or their personal responsibility, in contrast to someone else. In 1 Chronicles 17:7, "I took you from the pasture" emphasizes God's personal action towards David: it is He alone who made this choice. Similarly, in Ezekiel 25:17, "I am the Lord" solemnly affirms divine identity in the face of the nations.
3. In divine speeches especially, this pronoun becomes an affirmation of presence and power: "I, I" (repeated) underscores the certainty and authority of the speaker.
H0589.origine: This pronoun comes from the primitive root of the verb "to be" in Hebrew (חיה, "khayah"). The word "ani" is the autonomous form of the subject personal pronoun. In biblical texts, it appears in two forms: the autonomous form "ani" (more emphatic, 803 occurrences) and the affixed or enclitic form, integrated into the verb (more common in everyday speech). The autonomous form is reserved for insistence or rhetorical clarity.
