H0589.emploi: This pronoun appears 803 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in direct speeches and divine words. In Genesis and Exodus, God constantly uses it to announce His saving acts: "I am the Lord," "I will do," "I have taken." It also appears in the mouths of patriarchs and kings. In Psalms 119:67, the psalmist uses it to personally testify to his repentance: "I went astray." In Leviticus, "I am holy" or "I am the Lord your God" regularly returns to remind of the identity and holiness of the One who legislates. The context changes the weight of the pronoun: in God's mouth, it carries absolute authority; in that of humans, it marks a conviction or personal responsibility.
H0589.portee: For the reader, this small word reminds that every divine word addresses with a personal presence and a precise intention. When God says "I," it is not a mere grammatical affirmation: it is the declaration of an acting presence and a commitment. Similarly, when a human says "I," they take responsibility for their actions. This pronoun invites the believer to listen to the personal voice of God and to recognize their own part in the covenant and obedience.

sens: Sea boat, large vessel
Fleet, group of boats
Merchant ship intended for long sea voyages
H0590.detail:
1. A ship is a sea boat built to navigate long distances: it is a vessel capable of transporting goods or passengers. Solomon built them at Ezion-Geber, and experienced sailors ensured their navigation (1 Kings 9:26-27).
2. The word also refers to the entire group of boats in a fleet, or the fleet itself: King Solomon had ships of Tarshish at sea, which went on commercial expeditions every three years (1 Kings 10:22).
3. More broadly, it is a sea vessel, whether for commerce or transport: the ships of Hiram brought gold, precious wood, and stones from Ophir (1 Kings 10:11).
H0590.origine: The Hebrew word אֳנִי (oni) is derived from ancient Semitic. It specifically designates the sea boat or vessel, as opposed to simple river boats. It is found in other Semitic languages with the same meaning. The biblical context links it to commercial navigation and maritime exploration.
H0590.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Bible, only to speak of royal or commercial ships: Solomon's ships in the Red Sea (1 Kings 9:26-27), those of Hiram who supplied gold and precious wood (1 Kings 10:11), and especially the great ships of Tarshish that traveled every three years (1 Kings 10:22). In each case, it refers to ocean-going boats, robust and distant. In Isaiah 33:21, the prophet imagines rivers so majestic and swift that no oared ship could navigate them, illustrating the magnitude and power evoked by this word.
H0590.portee: The ship reminds the believer of faith in God in the face of the perils of the sea and distance: sailors entrusted their lives to storms and unknown distances. This biblical image of the ship speaks of risk, adventure, and trust in divine providence; it also evokes the wealth and power of a wise king who dared to explore the known world. For Isaiah, it magnifies the creative power of God, whose protection surpasses even the unleashed forces of nature.

sens: Sea vessel capable of navigating offshore
Merchant vessel intended for long voyages
Seaman, sailor
The crew or the entire fleet of ships
H0591.detail:
1. A ship is a large boat built to cross seas and oceans, unlike a simple boat. When Jonah flees from God, he goes down to Joppa, finds a ship going to Tarshish, pays his fare, and boards (Jonah 1:3).
2. The term particularly designates a merchant vessel used for trade and exploration: kings like Solomon and Jehoshaphat built ships of Tarshish (renowned eastern ports) to seek gold and riches (1 Kings 22:49, 2 Chronicles 20:36).
3. By extension, the word can also refer to the sailors themselves, the men who navigate and operate the ship. Thus, "sailor" also translates this same word in some passages.
4. In poetry or solemn language, "ships" can evoke an entire fleet or the collection of vessels of a people or an era, like the ships of Tarshish that symbolize commercial power.
H0591.origine: The Hebrew word אנייה (onyah) designates the ship as a floating object. This form comes from an ancient root related to the idea of carrying or maritime transport. The word appears in biblical texts with a certain nobility, often associated with the feat of navigation or distant trade. It stands in contrast to simple boats or small vessels and always retains the image of significant construction and a large-scale endeavor.
H0591.emploi: The word ship appears about 28 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical books, Psalms, and the prophets. It regularly designates the boats that the kings of Judah built for distant trade (Solomon in 1 Kings 9:27, Jehoshaphat in 1 Kings 22:49). The prophets mention the ships of Tarshish to symbolize the wealth and human power that God will humble (Isaiah 2:16). In Psalm 104, it is almost poetically that the psalmist imagines the ships sailing on the waves among the sea creatures. The book of Jonah features an ordinary ship facing a storm, showing the fragility of humanity in the face of God's will.
H0591.portee: The ship in Scripture symbolizes human ambition, distant enterprise, prosperous trade — and sometimes the pride that must be recognized as vain. For Jonah, it is the first instrument of his flight: boarding a ship represents believing one can escape God, an illusion that the storm destroys. For the believer, the ship reminds us that our most solid constructions, our farthest projects remain under the gaze and direction of the Lord.

sens: A painful sound made by someone who is suffering
An audible expression of pain, sadness, or mourning
Lamentation, prolonged complaint
H0592.detail: 1. Groaning is primarily a sound produced by a person in the throes of physical or emotional suffering: it is like a muffled cry, a painful murmur that escapes involuntarily. 2. In biblical passages, this word particularly denotes the collective expression of pain and mourning: Lamentations 2:5 speaks of the "daughter of Judah" filled with "groanings," meaning an entire city engulfed in sorrow and lamentation. 3. Groaning can also evoke a prolonged complaint, a ritual lamentation during mourning or in the face of calamity: in Isaiah 29:2, God announces that He will besiege Ariel and that there will be "complaints and groanings," images of disaster and suffering that will invade the city.
H0592.origine: The Hebrew word אֲנִיָּה (aniyyah) comes from a root expressing the idea of lamenting or groaning. It is related to other Hebrew words that denote complaint and pain. Its basic image is that of a painful sound arising from human distress, particularly in the context of mourning and calamity.
H0592.emploi: This word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Isaiah 29:2, it appears in a prophecy where God announces that He will besiege the holy city and fill it with groanings and complaints: an image of divine judgment. In Lamentations 2:5, it describes the state of Jerusalem after its destruction, filled with groanings and complaints. In both contexts, groaning expresses not only individual pain but also the collective affliction of a city, a people struck by misfortune.
H0592.portee: Groaning reminds us that suffering has a voice and cries out to God. This word also shows that mourning and lamentation are realities that God acknowledges and takes into account, and that the collective pain of a people does not escape His attention, even in judgment.

sens: Man of the tribe of Manasseh
H0593.detail: Aniam is a man of the tribe of Manasseh, living during the time of Egypt and the desert. He is the son of Shemida and the brother of Ahian, Shechem, and Likhi. His name appears only once in the Bible, in the genealogical record of 1 Chronicles 7:19, where he is listed among the sons of Shemida.
H0593.origine: The name Aniam literally means "I am the people" or can also be interpreted as "lamentation of the people." It is a Hebrew name composed reflecting a reality or circumstance particular to the time of his birth, according to the ancient custom of naming children to commemorate an event or express a sentiment.
H0593.emploi: Aniam is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:19, in the detailed genealogy of the tribe of Manasseh. He is listed among the four sons of Shemida, along with his brothers Ahian, Shechem, and Likhi. This brief mention indicates that he was a man of the tribe of Manasseh during the period of Egypt and the desert, but the Bible does not report any particular events concerning him.

sens: Plumb line or stretched cord used to check verticality and alignment in construction
Measuring and control instrument for straightness
Measure or standard of evaluation, in a figurative sense
H0594.detail: 1. The word primarily refers to a weighted line (often made of lead) that is allowed to hang to check that walls, doors, or other structures are straight: it is a tool of the mason and carpenter. In Amos 7:7, the Lord holds this plumb line in His hand, as if to inspect His work. 2. By extension, it is a cord or rule used to measure and control alignment — in verse 7, the wall itself is pulled with a line, emphasizing the expected precision. 3. Figuratively, the plumb line becomes a measure or standard of evaluation: when God places the plumb line in the midst of Israel (Amos 7:8), He measures the people according to a criterion of uprightness and justice, preparing for His judgment.
H0594.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of direction and exact measurement. The tool of the plumb line was well known to ancient builders of the Middle East; its use in the vision of Jeremiah and especially Amos makes it a powerful symbol of control and evaluation. The metaphor of the plumb line for judging moral uprightness and rectitude is characteristic of the prophetic tradition.
H0594.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the same prophetic passage: Amos 7:7-8. It is a vision received by the prophet Amos, where God shows him the Lord inspecting Israel with a plumb line in His hand. The prophetic context enriches the meaning: the plumb line ceases to be a mere technical tool to become the instrument of an unyielding divine judgment. The repetition of the word in verses 7 and 8 (the wall is pulled with a line, God places the plumb line) creates a strong unity of image.
H0594.portee: This image of the plumb line challenges the believer regarding God's judgment. It teaches that God evaluates obedience and justice according to an absolute and impartial measure — not based on appearance or promises, but on actual uprightness. For the people of Israel, it was a serious warning: judgment was imminent. For us, it reminds us that God will not judge based on our excuses, but according to His standard of justice, and that only grace in Christ lifts us up.

sens: The one who speaks, who states something in the first person
Marks self-affirmation before God or others
Expresses personal commitment or responsibility of the speaker
H0595.detail: 1. The word simply designates the person speaking, the one who says "I." It is the simplest form of the personal pronoun. In Genesis 3:10, Adam says, "I heard Your voice": he identifies himself as the one who acted. 2. This word allows the speaker to affirm his identity, authority, or role before someone else. When Moses says in Exodus 3:11, "Who am I to go to Pharaoh?" he uses this "I" to emphasize his own weakness and uncertainty. Similarly, in Exodus 20:2, God says, "I am the Lord your God," clearly affirming who He is. 3. It also marks personal commitment and responsibility. When Hannah says in 1 Samuel 1:15, "I have neither drunk wine nor strong drink," she personally calls upon her integrity as a witness. When Jeremiah announces, "I bring evil from the north" (4:6), he asserts that it is he who bears this divine message with all his authority.
H0595.origine: This word is an ancient and solemn form of the pronoun "I" in Hebrew. There is another more common form, "ani" (אֲנִי), but this word "anokhi" (אָֽנֹכִ֫י) gives a more emphatic or formal tone. It is particularly frequent at important moments: in God's words, in solemn moments, or when someone wants to emphasize themselves. This word does not come from another root; it is a primitive pronoun, ancient in the Hebrew language.
H0595.emploi: This word appears more than 330 times in the Old Testament. It is found throughout the Hebrew Bible, but especially in Genesis (where the patriarchs speak a lot about themselves), in Exodus (where God and Moses express themselves), and in prophetic words. It is used both when a man speaks of himself and when God designates Himself: "I am the Lord" (Exodus 20:2). In laws and commandments, it is often found at moments when authority is asserted or when someone takes responsibility.
H0595.portee: This small word reminds the reader of the importance of the person speaking: everyone is responsible for their actions, words, and faith. When the Bible uses this "I," it gives a personal and direct voice — that of the one who acts, who promises, who testifies. For the believer, this means that he cannot remain distant: he must hear the voice of God saying "I," and respond himself with his own "I" in faith and obedience.

sens: To complain in a low voice, grumbling, without openly rebelling
To contest, criticize the established order or someone's authority
To pity oneself, to lament one's fate
H0596.detail:
1. To murmur is primarily to express dissatisfaction through muffled words, grumblings: the people of Israel in the desert "murmur" against Moses and the Lord (Numbers 11:1), not through open rebellion, but through a rising resentment. It is a muted protest, almost involuntary.
2. This murmuring is also a form of contestation: by complaining, one implicitly questions the authority of the one in command. In the eyes of the Lord, the murmuring of the people is insubordination, as it expresses doubt towards His guidance and promises.
3. Finally, to complain is also to focus on one's own misfortune: in Lamentations 3:39, the wise man asks, "Why should anyone complain?" to invite reflection on one's faults rather than one's discomfort, for true wisdom is to recognize one's sin, not to pity oneself.
H0596.origine: The Hebrew verb אָנַן (anan) comes from a root that evokes a dull sound, the murmur of protest. It belongs to a field of words describing complaints and groans. The form used here (Hithpael) is reflexive: it suggests an action one does in relation to oneself, hence the idea of complaining, of allowing one's dissatisfaction to be expressed.
H0596.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible in the provided passages. In Numbers 11:1, it is the hungry people in the desert who murmur against their fate and against their leader: it is an act of rebellion described as offensive to the Lord, who responds with His fire. In Lamentations 3:39, the context is very different: the poet wonders if a living person should complain, then calls everyone to complain instead about their own sins — in other words, to repent rather than to whine. Murmuring is never valued in these two usages: it is either insubordination towards God or a lack of wisdom.
H0596.portee: Murmuring reveals the state of the heart: it betrays a lack of trust in God and His provision. For the Christian, this word invites examination of one's complaints — are they just indignation, or mere selfishness? — and to recognize that lamenting one's fate without repenting is a form of rebellion. Lamentations 3:39 teaches that true wisdom consists in transforming one's complaints into confession of sins.

sens: To compel someone to do something against their will
To constrain, impose by force
H0597.detail:
1. To compel someone to do something against their will: the word describes the action of forcing a person, pushing them to act without regard for their wishes. In Esther 1:8, King Ahasuerus did not force anyone to drink wine at his banquet, allowing everyone the freedom to choose — which shows that "to force" means to impose an act without consent.
2. To constrain, impose by force: this is the more general idea of constraint: one prevents someone from following their own will, subjecting them to an obligation they did not choose. The context of Esther highlights the contrast: a wise king does not force his guests, he respects their freedom.
H0597.origine: The Hebrew verb אָנַס (anas) comes from a root that expresses the idea of imposing, physically or morally constraining. Aramaic borrows the same root in the form אֲנַס (anas), which shows the antiquity and stability of the word in Semitic languages. The verb always evokes pressure, an external force that removes someone's freedom to act according to their choice.
H0597.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Esther 1:8. It is used in the negative form: the king did not force his guests. This context of a royal feast shows that "to force" opposes freedom and respect for individual will. The word emphasizes a principle of wisdom: true authority can also choose not to constrain. The unique appearance of the verb in this context of royal moderation gives it a particular moral significance.
H0597.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on the nature of authority: forcing is not always the right path. The king who does not force his subjects to drink shows a form of wisdom and respect. For the Christian, this reminds us that God invites without coercing, that faith is not imposed from the outside, and that true power often lies in respecting the freedom of others.

sens: That poses an obstacle, that does not yield easily
That exceeds ordinary capacity
That requires special effort or resistance
H0598.detail: 1. The word first evokes something that opposes, blocks the way, constrains — like a closed door that cannot be forced. In Daniel 4:9, when Nebuchadnezzar says that no secret is "difficult" for Daniel, he means: no secret resists him, escapes him, can block or embarrass him. 2. More broadly, it is what demands extra effort, a capacity beyond the ordinary — what exceeds, what surpasses. For God and His wise ones, nothing is difficult in the sense that everything yields, everything opens, everything is penetrable. 3. The word can also designate something that imposes a burden, a constraint: something harsh, rough, resistant.
H0598.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the Hebrew root אָנַס (anas), which means "to constrain, to force, to oppress" — the basic image is that of constraint, of violence that forces something. The root evokes the idea of something that opposes by force and must be overcome. In Aramaic, it has taken on the broader meaning of "difficult," that is, what opposes resistance and requires mastery.
H0598.emploi: This word appears only once in the Aramaic Bible, in Daniel 4:9. Nebuchadnezzar, impressed by Daniel's wisdom and supernatural gifts, states that no secret is difficult for him — he recognizes in the prophet a mysterious ability to uncover what remains hidden to others. It is a tribute to his exceptional power: Daniel possesses a superhuman ability to solve the inexplicable. The royal and prophetic context gives the word a solemn significance.
H0598.portee: This word reminds us that for one who possesses wisdom and the Spirit of God, the mysteries that seem impenetrable to ordinary man become accessible. Daniel represents the believer whose understanding is illuminated by God: nothing is "difficult" for one who lives in communion with the Most High. It is an invitation to recognize that our human limits are not the limits of God or of those He fills with His Spirit.

sens: To be angry, to feel a strong irritation
To breathe heavily due to rage
To be provoked to irritation by an offense or disobedience
To turn away from someone in anger
H0599.detail: 1. The word describes the emotional state of one who becomes angry: a rising anger, an indignation in response to what displeases (Psalms 60:3: "You have become angry"). 2. The primary image is that of heavy and loud breathing, characteristic of fury: one who becomes angry "breathes hard," like someone out of control. 3. The anger expressed by this verb is almost always provoked by a fault, a transgression: God becomes angry when the people violate His commandments (Deuteronomy 9:8: "You provoked the anger of the Lord"). 4. This divine irritation has serious consequences: it manifests as punishment, abandonment, or the threat of destruction (2 Kings 17:18: "The Lord was very angry with Israel, and He removed them from His presence").
H0599.origine: The Hebrew verb אָנַף (anaph) derives from a root that expresses the idea of "to blow," "to breathe heavily." This image of angry breathing is common in Semitic languages and reinforces the idea that anger is a visceral emotion that grips the whole body. The related noun אַף (aph) literally means "nose" or "nostrils," reminding us that it is through the nose that the furious breath escapes. This etymology explains why Hebrew often speaks of "anger" by saying "the irritation of the nose."
H0599.emploi: The verb אָנַף appears 14 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively to express God's anger. It arises in contexts of transgression: God becomes angry with Moses because of the people's rebellion (Deuteronomy 1:37), against the people themselves at Sinai (Deuteronomy 9:8), against the kings who turn away from His Law (1 Kings 11:9). The psalmist also cries out to God to cease being angry (Psalms 79:5; Psalms 85:6). The word expresses a firm and lasting anger, not a fleeting outburst, and it always carries a moral weight: God becomes angry only against evil, never without reason.
H0599.portee: This word reveals that God's anger is not a blind passion, but a just reaction to disobedience and sin. It invites the believer to take divine commandments seriously, knowing that God does not remain indifferent to our actions. It is also an invitation to repentance: to recognize that we have provoked God by our sins and to seek His grace to escape His judgment.

sens: Village de Ruben situé près de Hesbon, en Transjordanie
H0500.detail: Élealé est une petite ville fortifiée du territoire de Ruben, dans la région de Hesbon, à l'est du Jourdain. Elle apparaît dans les listes de villes que la tribu de Ruben a bâties et fortifiées après la conquête de Canaan (Numbers 32:37). Dans les prophéties contre Moab (Isaiah 15 et 16, Jeremiah 48), Élealé est mentionnée aux côtés de Hesbon comme l'une des villes qui subiront les ravages de la guerre et dont les habitants crieront de détresse, ce qui suggère une ville prospère avec des vignobles et une vie agricole florissante.
H0500.origine: Le nom signifie « Dieu est ascendant » ou « Dieu s'élève » : il combine le nom de Dieu (El) et le verbe exprimant l'ascension ou l'élévation. C'est un nom théophore typique de la région syro-palestinienne, reflétant la foi des habitants en la puissance divine. Aucun lien étymologique spécifique ne relie ce nom à d'autres termes hébreux courants.
H0500.emploi: Élealé apparaît cinq fois dans la Bible hébraïque, exclusivement dans l'Ancien Testament. Elle est d'abord citée dans Numbers 32 comme l'une des villes que les fils de Ruben ont construites et fortifiées après avoir reçu leur héritage en Transjordanie. Par la suite, elle figure dans trois oracles prophétiques contre Moab (Isaiah 15:4, Isaiah 16:9, Jeremiah 48:34), où elle est systématiquement associée à Hesbon. Ces prophéties décrivent les cris de guerre, les lamentations et les ravages qui fondront sur ces villes lors des invasions. Élealé incarne une ville frontalière prospère, exposée aux conflits régionaux et vulnérable aux incursions étrangères.
H0500.portee: Élealé rappelle au lecteur que les terres promises incluaient non seulement Canaan proprement dite, mais aussi les territoires de Transjordanie, où les tribus d'Israël se sont établies. Son nom théophore témoigne de la foi en Dieu des anciens habitants. Les prophéties qui la mentionnent illustrent comment le jugement divin s'exerce sur les nations environnantes et comment aucune ville, aussi prospère soit-elle, n'est à l'abri de la conséquence de l'infidélité et du péché.

sens: descendant de Juda, fils de Hélets
ancêtre de Sismaï dans la généalogie de Juda
H0501G.detail:
1. Élasa est un homme de la tribu de Juda qui apparaît dans la généalogie royale. Il est le fils de Hélets et le père de Sismaï, comme l'indique la liste des ancêtres du peuple d'Israël en 1 Chronicles 2:39-40.
2. Son nom apparaît seulement dans cette chaîne généalogique, qui retrace la descendance de Juda à travers plusieurs générations. Il occupe une place modeste mais certaine dans l'histoire du peuple élu.
H0501G.origine: Le nom Élasa signifie « Dieu a fait » ou « Dieu a créé ». Il est formé de deux éléments : « Él » qui désigne Dieu en hébreu, et une racine évoquant l'action de créer ou de faire. Ce nom exprime la confiance que Dieu accomplit ses desseins et crée ce qui est nécessaire pour son peuple.
H0501G.emploi: Élasa est mentionné deux fois dans la Bible, uniquement dans 1 Chronicles 2:39-40, où apparaît une généalogie du clan de Juda. Ces deux versets consécutifs situent Élasa entre son père Hélets et son fils Sismaï, ce qui en fait un maillon de la chaîne généalogique par laquelle le peuple de Juda se rattache à ses ancêtres. Ce type de généalogie servait à établir l'identité et l'héritage des familles israélites.

sens: Homme de la tribu de Benjamin à l'époque de la monarchie divisée
H0501H.detail: Éleasa est un descendant de Benjamin, fils de Rapha et père d'Atsel, mentionné dans les généalogies du peuple d'Israël. Il appartient à la tribu de Benjamin et vit pendant la période de la monarchie divisée. Son nom apparaît deux fois dans les registres généalogiques de 1 Chronicles, d'abord en 8:37 et ensuite en 9:43, dans une liste des descendants de Benjamin.
H0501H.origine: Le nom Éleasa signifie « Dieu a créé » ou « Dieu a fait ». Il est composé de deux éléments hébreux : « El » (Dieu) et « asah » (faire, créer). Ce nom théophore exprime la conviction que Dieu est l'auteur de la vie et reflète la foi des parents hébreux en la création divine.
H0501H.emploi: Éleasa est mentionné deux fois dans les généalogies de 1 Chronicles. Il apparaît d'abord en 1 Chronicles 8:37 comme fils de Rapha et père d'Atsel, dans une liste généalogique de la tribu de Benjamin. Le même Éleasa est mentionné à nouveau en 1 Chronicles 9:43, dans une répétition de cette même généalogie. Ces deux passages nous montrent qu'Éleasa s'inscrit dans une lignée benjaminite bien établie, mais la Bible ne nous donne aucun détail sur sa vie personnelle ou ses actions.

sens: Prêtre de la ligne de Paschhur qui avait épousé une femme étrangère du temps d'Esdras
H0501I.detail: Éleasa est un prêtre appartenant à la descendance de Paschhur, un lignage sacerdotal établi. Au temps d'Esdras, il figurait parmi ceux qui avaient contracté mariage avec des femmes étrangères (non israélites), ce qui posait un problème théologique et pratique pour la pureté de la communauté restaurée après l'exil à Babylone. Son nom apparaît dans la liste de ceux qui ont dû se séparer de leurs épouses étrangères afin de restaurer la séparation d'Israël (Ezra 10:22).
H0501I.origine: Le nom Éleasa signifie « Dieu a fait » ou « Dieu a créé », composé de la racine divine « El » (Dieu) et du verbe « asah » (faire, créer). C'est un nom théophore courant en hébreu, qui exprime la confiance en l'action créatrice et bienfaisante de Dieu. La même personne peut aussi être appelée Eljoénaï dans certains contextes.
H0501I.emploi: Éleasa est mentionné une seule fois dans la Bible, en Ezra 10:22, dans le contexte des réformes religieuses menées par Esdras après le retour d'exil. Il figure sur la liste des prêtres et lévites qui s'étaient unis à des femmes d'origine non juive. Cette énumération montre que le problème des mariages mixtes touchait aussi les classes sacerdotales, et que la restauration religieuse exigeait de ces hommes, notamment des prêtres, une rupture avec ces alliances.
H0501I.portee: La mention d'Éleasa rappelle que le retour d'exil a imposé des choix difficiles et des mesures rigoureuses pour préserver l'identité religieuse d'Israël. Elle invite à réfléchir à la tension entre miséricorde et séparation, entre l'accueil et la pureté religieuse, dans les périodes de restauration spirituelle.

sens: Fils de Schaphan, serviteur du roi Sédécias de Juda
H0501J.detail: Éleasa est un homme de haut rang à la cour royale de Juda au moment du règne de Sédécias, peu avant la chute de Jérusalem. Il est le fils de Schaphan, une famille de scribes et de conseillers influents. Dans le seul passage où il est nommé, il est envoyé en mission diplomatique à Babylone auprès du roi Nabuchodonosor, porteur d'une lettre du prophète Jérémie adressée aux exilés (Jeremiah 29:3). Cette mission montre qu'il jouissait de la confiance du roi et qu'il occupait une position importante dans l'administration du royaume.
H0501J.origine: Le nom Éleasa signifie « Dieu a fait » ou « Dieu a créé », composé de l'élément divin El (Dieu) et d'une forme verbale exprimant l'action de créer ou de faire. C'est un nom théophore typique de l'hébreu ancien, qui exprime une confiance envers l'action bénéfique de Dieu.
H0501J.emploi: Éleasa n'apparaît qu'une seule fois dans la Bible, en Jeremiah 29:3. Il y est présenté comme l'un des deux messagers envoyés par le roi Sédécias de Juda vers Nabuchodonosor, roi de Babylone. Son compagnon de mission est Guemaria, fils du prophète Hilkija. Ensemble, ils portent une lettre du prophète Jérémie destinée aux captifs judéens déportés à Babylone, lettre qui les encourage à accepter leur sort et à prier pour la paix de la ville de leur exil. Cette mention unique révèle l'importance d'Éleasa dans la correspondance politique et prophétique d'une période critique de l'histoire de Juda.
H0501J.portee: La présence d'Éleasa aux côtés de Guemaria montre comment Dieu utilisait même les serviteurs du roi pour transmettre son message prophétique aux exilés. Bien que Sédécias ne soit pas toujours demeuré fidèle aux paroles de Jérémie, le fait que sa cour ait assuré la transmission de ce message révèle la providence divine dans les événements politiques. Pour le lecteur, cela rappelle que même en période de crise ou d'exil, Dieu maintient un canal de communication avec son peuple et veille à ce que sa parole parvienne à ceux qui ont besoin de l'entendre.
